Before You Begin

Welcome! This book takes you from your very first line of JavaScript to real programs that run in the browser. You do not need any programming experience. If you know a little HTML and CSS, you are ready to start.

How every idea is taught

Each new idea in this book is explained in the same eight steps, always in the same order. Once you know the labels, you always know where to look.

Label What you will find
What is it? The idea in very simple words
Why do we use it? The real purpose: what problem it solves
Syntax The basic pattern you type
Simple example The smallest example that works
Real-world example How it is used in something real
Common mistakes The traps almost every beginner falls into
Key points Three to six things to remember
Practice Small exercises to try yourself

Between the ideas you will find boxes with extra help, and at the end of each chapter a mini project where you build something real. At the end of each part there is a bigger project that combines everything you learned.

Type the code yourself

Do not copy and paste. Typing each example, even a short one, teaches your fingers and your brain at the same time. When something breaks, that is good news: you are learning what the error means.

About the output blocks

The green Output blocks show what the program prints when you run it with Node.js. In the browser console the same result may look a little different (for example, arrays and objects can have small arrows and extra labels). The values are always the same.

What you need

  • A web browser. Chrome, Edge, or Firefox all work. Press F12 to open the developer tools and click the Console tab.
  • A code editor. Visual Studio Code is free and popular. Any plain text editor will also work.
  • A folder for your work. Create one folder called js-book and keep everything from this book inside it.
  • Node.js (optional). It lets you run JavaScript from a terminal. You can learn every idea in this book with only a browser.

How to get the most out of this book

  1. Read a section, then close the book and try to explain it in your own words.
  2. Run every example, then change something and predict what will happen.
  3. Do the practice exercises before you look at the sample answers.
  4. When an error appears, read the message slowly. It usually tells you the problem and the line number.
  5. Take breaks. Understanding one small thing well is better than rushing through five.

The road ahead

  • Part 1: JavaScript fundamentals. Variables, data types, operators, conditions, loops, and functions. These are the building blocks of every program.
  • Part 2: Working with data. Arrays, objects, strings, and numbers. You will learn to store, search, and transform information.
  • Part 3: JavaScript in the browser. The DOM and events. You will make real web pages that react to clicks, typing, and more.

At the end of each part, you will also build a bigger project that combines everything from that part. Mini projects at the end of chapters give you smaller practice along the way.

Ready? Turn to Chapter 1.

Chapter 1

What is JavaScript?

Every website you use does two jobs: it shows you things, and it reacts when you do something. Clicking a heart, typing in a search box, playing a game in the browser: all of that reacting is done by JavaScript. In this chapter you will meet the language and run your first program.

What you will learn

  • What JavaScript is and why people use it
  • How JavaScript, HTML, and CSS are different
  • Where JavaScript runs: the browser and Node.js
  • How the computer reads your code
  • How to print messages with console.log()
  • How to write and run your first program

1.1What is JavaScript?

What is it?

JavaScript (often shortened to JS) is a programming language. A programming language is a way of giving instructions to a computer, using words and symbols the computer can follow.

You already know two languages of the web. Think of a web page as a house:

Language Its job In a house
HTML Structure: what is on the page Walls, doors, and rooms
CSS Style: how the page looks Paint, curtains, and furniture
JavaScript Behavior: what the page does Electricity: lights switch on, the doorbell rings

HTML and CSS describe a page. JavaScript makes it act.

Why do we use it?

We use JavaScript to make pages interactive. It can show or hide a menu, check a form before it is sent, update the score in a game, or load new posts without refreshing the page. JavaScript also runs outside the browser, so people use it to build servers, mobile apps, and desktop apps too.

Syntax

JavaScript goes inside a <script> tag in your HTML file:

Later you will keep JavaScript in its own file and link it (you will see how in Section 1.4).

Simple example

Here is a tiny page where HTML, CSS, and JavaScript each do their own job:

The HTML says "Hello!", but JavaScript changes the text the moment the page loads. You see Hello from JavaScript! in blue.

Do not worry yet

You cannot read document.querySelector(...) yet, and that is fine. You will learn it in Chapter 12. For now, just see the idea: JavaScript can change a page.

Real-world example

Have you ever seen "Password too short" appear while you type a password? That is JavaScript checking your input. Here is the idea in a few lines (you will learn if properly in Chapter 5):

Common mistakes

  • Thinking JavaScript and Java are the same language. They are different languages that only share part of a name.
  • Writing JavaScript straight into the page without a <script> tag. The browser will just show it as text.
  • Trying to memorize everything at once. Programmers look things up all the time. Understanding matters more than memorizing.

Key points

  • JavaScript is a programming language that makes web pages interactive.
  • HTML is structure, CSS is style, and JavaScript is behavior.
  • In an HTML page, JavaScript lives inside a <script> tag.
  • JavaScript also runs outside the browser, for example on servers.

Practice

  1. Explain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to a friend using the house idea (or a better idea of your own).
  2. Write down three things on a website that must be done by JavaScript, not by HTML or CSS.
  3. Save the example above as hello.html, open it in a browser, and change the heading color and the message.
Did you know?

JavaScript was created in 1995 by Brendan Eich in about ten days, for the Netscape browser. Today it runs on billions of devices.

1.2Where Does JavaScript Run?

What is it?

JavaScript code needs a program that can read it and follow the instructions. That program is called a JavaScript engine. You can find an engine in two common places:

  • The browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari). Every browser has an engine inside. Chrome's engine is called V8.
  • Node.js, a free program that lets you run JavaScript on your own computer, outside the browser. Node.js uses the same V8 engine as Chrome.

The language is the same in both places. What changes is the extra tools each place gives you:

Feature Browser Node.js
Extra tools document, window, alert(): tools to control web pages Tools to read and write files and build servers
Good for Interactive web pages Servers, command-line tools, automation
How you run code Open a page, or type in the console node file.js in a terminal

Why do we use it?

Knowing where your code runs tells you which tools you can use. Browser JavaScript can change a web page. Node.js JavaScript can create files or run a web server. Beginners usually start in the browser, because you see the result right away.

Syntax

There are two common ways to run a JavaScript file:

You can also type JavaScript directly into the Console of your browser: press F12, open the Console tab, type a line, and press Enter.

Simple example

Open your browser, press F12, click the Console tab, type the line below, and press Enter:

The console understands JavaScript, so it works like a very smart calculator.

Real-world example

In the browser, JavaScript powers the "like" button, search suggestions, and online quizzes. In Node.js, JavaScript can power the server that checks your login and sends the right page, or a small tool that renames a thousand files in one go.

Common mistakes

  • Using browser-only tools such as document or alert() in Node.js. You will get an error, because Node.js has no web page.
  • Forgetting to save the file before running it. The old version runs instead.
  • Thinking you must install Node.js first. You can learn everything in this book with just a browser.

Key points

  • JavaScript runs inside an engine, either in a browser or in Node.js.
  • The language is the same everywhere. The extra tools are different.
  • The browser is great for pages and buttons. Node.js is great for servers and file tools.
  • Press F12 in your browser to open the console.

Practice

  1. Open the console in your browser and type 10 * 5. What do you see?
  2. Which one needs a browser: changing a heading's color, or reading a file from your computer?
  3. (Optional) Install Node.js from nodejs.org, then type node -v in a terminal to see its version number.

1.3How JavaScript Works (A High-Level Look)

What is it?

When you run JavaScript, this is what happens:

The engine reads your code from top to bottom, one statement at a time. A statement is one instruction, like one step in a recipe. The engine translates each step into something the computer understands, and the computer does it.

JavaScript also does one thing at a time, like a cashier who serves one customer at a time.

Why do we use it?

This top-to-bottom rule explains many beginner errors. If you use something before you create it, the engine has not met it yet, so it does not know what you mean.

Syntax

Each statement usually sits on its own line and ends with a semicolon ;.

Simple example

The steps run in exactly the order you wrote them.

Real-world example

Think of a recipe: crack the egg, whisk it, then cook it. Change the order and you get a mess. Code is the same. Here is what happens when you use a name the engine has not met yet:

The fix is to create it first, then use it:

Common mistakes

  • Using a value before creating it. You will see an error like playerName is not defined.
  • Expecting the engine to guess what you meant. It follows exactly what you wrote, nothing more.
  • Ignoring error messages. Read them slowly: they usually tell you the line number and the problem.

Key points

  • The engine reads code from top to bottom, one statement at a time.
  • Order matters. Create things before you use them.
  • Error messages are helpers, not enemies.
  • JavaScript does one thing at a time.

Practice

  1. Predict the output before you run it: three lines that print "A", then "B", then "C".
  2. Write four console.log lines that describe the steps of making tea, in the right order.
  3. Swap two of the lines. Does the program break, or does only the order of the output change?

1.4Your First Program: console.log()

What is it?

console.log() prints a message to the console, a special screen where developers see what their program says. Text goes inside quotes. Text inside quotes is called a string (you will study strings in Chapter 3).

Why do we use it?

You cannot see inside your program while it runs. console.log() is your window into it. You use it to check that your code works and to hunt for bugs, and you will use it almost every day.

Syntax

console is the tool, .log is the action, the brackets ( ) hold what you want to print, and ; ends the statement.

Simple example

Text needs quotes, numbers do not, and commas let you print several things on one line, separated by spaces.

Real-world example

Programmers use console.log() to check their work. Imagine a shop program that calculates a bill. To see whether the total is right, print it:

You will meet let in the next chapter. For now, read it as "store the number 250 in a box called price".

Common mistakes

  • Writing Console.log or console.Log. JavaScript is case-sensitive: capital letters matter.
  • Forgetting the quotes around text. In console.log(Hello), JavaScript thinks Hello is a name and fails.
  • Forgetting a closing bracket or quote. Every ( needs a ) and every opening quote needs a closing quote.

Key points

  • console.log() prints values to the console.
  • Put text inside quotes. Numbers do not need quotes.
  • Separate several values with commas.
  • JavaScript is case-sensitive.

Practice

  1. Print your name.
  2. Print three lines: your favorite food, your favorite color, and your favorite subject.
  3. Print the result of 15 * 4, and then print the sentence "15 times 4 is" followed by the result on the same line.
Comments: notes for humans

Anything after // on a line is a comment. The engine ignores it, so you can use comments to explain your code.

Mini project: Hello, Console!

Build a tiny web page that greets you in the console. You will use two files, just like a real project.

  1. Make a folder called js-book. Inside it, create a file named index.html:
  1. In the same folder, create script.js:
  1. Open index.html in your browser, press F12, and click the Console tab. Your three messages appear.

Challenge: add three more lines about yourself. Then break something on purpose (for example, delete a closing quote), reload, and read the error message.

Chapter 1 in one minute
  • JavaScript makes web pages interactive: HTML is structure, CSS is style, JavaScript is behavior.
  • It runs in an engine, inside the browser or inside Node.js.
  • The engine reads your code from top to bottom, one statement at a time.
  • console.log() shows values in the console, and it is your best debugging friend.
  • JavaScript is case-sensitive, and error messages are there to help you.

Chapter 2

Variables

Programs need to remember things: your score in a game, the name you typed, the price of an item. A variable is how a program remembers. In this chapter you will learn how to create variables, change them, protect them, and give them good names.

What you will learn

  • What a variable is and how to create one
  • The difference between let, const, and var
  • How to change (reassign) a variable
  • Which values should be constants
  • The rules and good habits for naming variables

2.1Variables with let

What is it?

A variable is a named box in the computer's memory. The name is the label on the box, and the value is what is inside. With let, you can look inside the box any time, and you can also put a new value inside.

Why do we use it?

A program without variables can only work with values you type directly into the code. Variables let you store a value once, use it many times, and change it while the program runs, like a score that goes up.

Syntax

let creates the variable. variableName is the label. The = sign means store (it does not mean "is equal to"). value is what goes into the box.

Simple example

You write let only the first time. After that, just use the name: score = 10;.

Real-world example

A game keeps a player's name and points. The points change as the game goes on:

Read points = points + 5 from right to left: take the old value (20), add 5, and store the answer (25) back in points.

Common mistakes

  • Writing let twice for the same name. The second let causes an error.
  • Reading = as "equals". In JavaScript, = means "store the value on the right into the box on the left".
  • Using a variable before you have created it.

Key points

  • A variable is a named box that holds a value.
  • Create it with let, and change it later without let.
  • = stores a value. It does not compare.
  • A variable must be created before you use it.

Practice

  1. Create a variable called age, print it, change it to a new number, and print it again.
  2. Create cups with the value 2. Add 1 to it and print the result.
  3. Create two variables, firstName and lastName, and print them on one line.

2.2Constants with const

What is it?

const creates a variable that cannot be changed after you give it a value. The word comes from "constant", which means "stays the same".

Why do we use it?

Some values should never change: the value of pi, a tax rate, the name of your website. With const, JavaScript protects you from changing them by accident, and it tells anyone reading your code, "this stays fixed". A good habit is to use const first, and switch to let only when the value really needs to change.

Syntax

Simple example

If you try to change it, JavaScript stops you:

Real-world example

A shop has a fixed tax rate, but the price changes for every item:

The tax rate is const because it never changes while the program runs. The price can change, so it uses let.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to change a const value. You get an error, and this is the protection working.
  • Creating a const without a value. const x; is an error, because you can never give it a value later.
  • Using const for something that must change, such as a score or a counter.

Key points

  • const creates a variable that cannot be reassigned.
  • It must get its value at the moment it is created.
  • Use const by default and let when the value will change.
  • Errors from const are helpful: they show you a mistake early.

Practice

  1. Create const daysInWeek = 7 and print it. Then try to change it and read the error message.
  2. Write a program that uses const pi and a let radius to print the area of a circle (pi * radius * radius).
  3. Decide: should each of these be let or const? A person's birthday, the number of items in a shopping cart, the name of your school.

2.3The Old Way: var

What is it?

var is the original way to create variables in JavaScript. It was the only way until 2015, when let and const arrived. It still works, but it has some confusing behavior.

Why do we use it?

You need to recognize var because you will see it in older tutorials and older code. But in your own code, use let and const.

Syntax

Simple example

Here is the biggest difference. A block is any code between curly brackets { }. A let variable stays inside its block, but a var variable leaks out:

Real-world example

Imagine a big program. Early on, a programmer writes var total = 100;. Two hundred lines later, someone else writes the same name again:

With let, the second line would give an error and warn you. That is why modern code avoids var.

Common mistakes

  • Using var out of habit. Choose let or const instead.
  • Expecting a var variable to stay inside { }. It does not.
  • Creating the same var twice by accident. JavaScript will not warn you.

Key points

  • var is the old way to create variables.
  • It ignores block boundaries, and it lets you create the same name twice.
  • Read it, but do not write it in new code.
  • Prefer const, and use let when the value changes.

Practice

  1. Rewrite var color = "red"; using let, and then using const.
  2. Run the "leaky" example, then change var to let and read the error.
  3. In your own words: why is it a problem when a variable "leaks" out of its block?

2.4Naming Variables

What is it?

A variable's name is called an identifier. JavaScript has strict rules (which you must follow) and there are good habits (which make your code easy to read).

Rules:

  • Use letters, digits, _, and $.
  • Do not start with a digit.
  • No spaces or dashes.
  • Do not use a reserved word such as let, const, if, or class.
  • Names are case-sensitive: age and Age are two different variables.

Good habits:

  • Use camelCase: start with a small letter and capitalize each new word (firstName, totalPrice).
  • Pick names that describe the value.
  • Start yes/no variables with is or has (isLoggedIn, hasPaid).
  • Write fixed settings in UPPER_CASE with underscores if you like (MAX_USERS).

Why do we use it?

Code is read many more times than it is written. A clear name like totalPrice explains itself, while x makes everyone guess, including you next week.

Syntax

Simple example

These names break the rules:

Real-world example

Compare two versions of the same shopping calculation. The second one explains itself:

Common mistakes

  • Mixing capital letters: totalMarks and totalmarks are different names, so one of them will cause a "not defined" error.
  • Using very short names (a, q) or meaningless names (data1, thing).
  • Using spaces or dashes. Write firstName, not first name or first-name.

Key points

  • Names may use letters, digits, _, and $, but cannot start with a digit.
  • Names are case-sensitive.
  • Use camelCase and descriptive names.
  • Start yes/no names with is or has.

Practice

  1. Which of these names are wrong, and why? user_name, 2ndPlayer, total price, isOnline, class
  2. Write good variable names for: a student's age, the price of a pen, whether a user has logged in.
  3. Rename this: let a = 15; let b = 4; let c = a * b; so it describes a rectangle's area.
Mini project: Student ID Card

Print a student ID card using variables. Some values are fixed (const), and others change (let).

Challenge 1: put your own details in the card.

Challenge 2 (a classic puzzle): you have two boxes, a = 5 and b = 8. Swap their values. You will need a third box to hold one value for a moment.

Chapter 2 in one minute
  • A variable is a named box that stores a value.
  • let for values that change, const for values that stay fixed, and avoid var.
  • = stores a value from the right into the name on the left.
  • Names are case-sensitive, use camelCase, and should describe the value.

Chapter 3

Data Types

Not every value is the same kind of thing. A name is text, an age is a number, and "Is the door open?" is a yes-or-no answer. JavaScript calls these kinds of values data types. Think of containers: a bottle holds water, a box holds shoes. Knowing the type of a value tells you what you can do with it.

What you will learn

  • The seven basic data types: string, number, boolean, undefined, null, BigInt, and symbol
  • How to write each type
  • Why "5" and 5 are not the same
  • How to check a type with typeof

3.1Strings

What is it?

A string is text: letters, digits, spaces, and symbols inside quotes. You can use double quotes "...", single quotes '...', or backticks.

Why do we use it?

Names, messages, emails, and addresses are all text. Almost every program works with strings.

Syntax

Backticks are special. They let you put values inside the text with ${ }. This is called a template literal.

Simple example

Joining strings with + is called concatenation. Template literals give the same result and are usually easier to read.

Real-world example

A website greets you and tells you about your messages:

Common mistakes

  • Starting with one kind of quote and ending with another: "Hello' is an error.
  • Forgetting quotes, so JavaScript treats your text as a variable name.
  • Thinking "5" is a number. Look at what + does with text:

Key points

  • A string is text inside quotes ("...", '...', or backticks).
  • Use + to join strings.
  • Backticks with ${ } put values inside text.
  • "5" is text, and 5 is a number.

Practice

  1. Create a string variable with your favorite movie, and print it.
  2. Use a template literal to print: My name is ..., and I am ... years old. using two variables.
  3. Predict, then check: what does "10" + "20" print? What about 10 + 20?

3.2Numbers

What is it?

The number type holds every kind of number: whole numbers like 15 and decimals like 99.5. JavaScript uses one type for both.

Why do we use it?

Prices, ages, scores, distances, and every calculation use numbers.

Syntax

Numbers never use quotes. Two special number values exist too: Infinity and NaN (which means "Not a Number", and you will meet it in Chapter 11).

Simple example

Real-world example

Four friends share a restaurant bill equally:

Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not 0.3?

Computers store decimals in binary, and some decimals cannot be stored exactly, just like 1/3 cannot be written exactly as a decimal. This happens in every programming language. In Chapter 11 you will learn how to round results neatly.

Common mistakes

  • Putting numbers in quotes ("15"). That is text, and it behaves differently.
  • Writing a comma inside a number (1,000). Use 1000 or 1_000.
  • Being surprised by tiny decimal errors such as 0.30000000000000004. It is normal.

Key points

  • One number type holds whole numbers and decimals.
  • Numbers do not use quotes.
  • NaN and Infinity are special number values.
  • Decimals can have tiny rounding errors.

Practice

  1. Create variables for the length and width of a room (numbers), and print its area.
  2. Print the result of 7 / 2. Is it what you expected?
  3. Split a bill of 950 between 5 people and print each share.

3.3Booleans

What is it?

A boolean has only two possible values: true or false (no quotes). It is like a light switch: on or off.

Why do we use it?

Programs make decisions, and decisions need yes-or-no answers: Is the user logged in? Is the password correct? Is the game over? Booleans store those answers.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A page decides what to show, depending on a boolean (you will learn if in Chapter 5):

Common mistakes

  • Writing "true" with quotes. That is a string, not a boolean.
  • Capital letters: True and FALSE are wrong. Write true and false.
  • Using confusing names. isLoggedIn is clearer than login.

Key points

  • A boolean is either true or false.
  • Never put quotes around them.
  • Comparisons such as 10 > 5 produce booleans.
  • Name booleans with is or has so they read like questions.

Practice

  1. Create isWeekend and hasHomework variables and print them.
  2. What does 5 > 8 print? What about 5 < 8?
  3. Write a boolean variable name for: "The user accepted the terms."

3.4undefined and null

What is it?

Both mean "no value", but in different ways.

  • undefined means the box was created, but nothing was put inside. JavaScript gives you this automatically.
  • null means the box is empty on purpose. You choose to write it.

Why do we use it?

Programs often need a value that means "nothing yet": a seat that no one has chosen, or a search that found no result.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A quiz app remembers which answer the player picked. Before they choose, it is null:

Common mistakes

  • Mixing them up. A good rule: undefined is "JavaScript did not get a value", null is "I decided there is no value".
  • Writing "null" in quotes. That is a string.
  • Being surprised by undefined when you forget to give a variable a value.

Key points

  • undefined means a variable exists but has no value yet.
  • null means "empty on purpose".
  • Both mean "nothing", but they are different types of values.
  • You usually write null yourself and let JavaScript create undefined.

Practice

  1. Create a variable with no value and print it. What do you see?
  2. Create currentUser with the value null, and then give it the value "Sam".
  3. Explain the difference between undefined and null in one sentence.

3.5BigInt and Symbol

What is it?

These are two special types that you will not need often.

  • BigInt holds very large whole numbers. Write an n at the end: 123n.
  • Symbol creates a value that is always unique. Even two symbols with the same description are different.

Why do we use it?

Normal numbers lose exact accuracy above about 9 quadrillion (9,007,199,254,740,991). BigInt keeps every digit exact. Symbols help advanced programs avoid name clashes.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A social app gives every post a 19-digit ID. As a normal number, the last digits could be wrong. As a BigInt, the ID stays exact:

Common mistakes

  • Mixing BigInt and normal numbers: 5n + 1 gives an error. Use 5n + 1n.
  • Forgetting the n at the end of a BigInt.
  • Expecting two symbols with the same description to be equal. They never are.

Key points

  • BigInt (123n) stores huge whole numbers exactly.
  • Symbol creates a unique value.
  • You cannot mix BigInt with normal numbers in one calculation.
  • Both are rare in beginner programs. Just know they exist.

Practice

  1. Create a BigInt with the value 500n and add 1n to it.
  2. What happens when you run console.log(5n + 1)? Read the error message.
  3. Create two symbols with the same description and compare them with ===.

3.6Checking a Type with typeof

What is it?

typeof is a tool that tells you the type of a value. It gives its answer as text.

Why do we use it?

When a program misbehaves, the cause is often a wrong type, such as "5" (text) instead of 5 (number). typeof lets you check quickly.

Syntax

Simple example

A famous quirk

typeof null gives "object". This is an old mistake in JavaScript that was never fixed, because fixing it would break old websites. null is not really an object. Just remember this special case.

Real-world example

Values that come from a web form are always text, even if the user typed a number. typeof helps you notice:

Common mistakes

  • Expecting typeof null to say "null".
  • Forgetting that the answer is a string. To compare, write typeof x === "number", with quotes.
  • Expecting typeof to separate arrays from objects. Both give "object" (you will see better tools in Chapter 8).

Key points

  • typeof returns the type of a value as text.
  • The types you know: "string", "number", "boolean", "undefined", "bigint", "symbol", and "object".
  • typeof null is "object", an old quirk.
  • Check types when a result looks strange.

Practice

  1. Use typeof on your name, your age, and false.
  2. What does typeof "42" print? Why is it not "number"?
  3. Predict the output of console.log(typeof typeof 5), then run it.
Mini project: Data Type Detective

Guess each type before you run the program. Then run it and check how many you got right.

Challenge: add three more mystery values of your own, such as a BigInt and a string with backticks, and predict their types.

Chapter 3 in one minute
  • Every value has a type: string, number, boolean, undefined, null, BigInt, or symbol.
  • Strings are text in quotes, and "5" is not the same as 5.
  • undefined means "no value yet", and null means "empty on purpose".
  • typeof tells you the type of a value. typeof null is "object", an old quirk.

4
Chapter 4

Operators

Think about the buttons on a calculator: plus, minus, times, divide. In JavaScript, symbols that do work with values are called operators. The values they work on are called operands. In 5 + 3, the + is the operator, and 5 and 3 are the operands. In this chapter you will learn the operators you will use in almost every program.

What you will learn

  • Do math with arithmetic operators, including modulus and exponentiation
  • Update variables quickly with assignment operators and ++ / --
  • Compare values, and know why === is better than ==
  • Combine yes-or-no answers with logical operators
  • Choose between two values with the ternary operator

4.1Arithmetic Operators

What is it?

Arithmetic operators do math. Two of them may be new to you: modulus (%) gives the remainder after a division, and exponentiation (**) means "to the power of".

Operator Meaning Example Result
+ Add 10 + 3 13
- Subtract 10 - 3 7
* Multiply 10 * 3 30
/ Divide 10 / 4 2.5
% Remainder (modulus) 10 % 3 1
** Power 2 ** 3 8

Why do we use it?

Every calculation in a program uses these: prices, totals, scores, areas. The remainder operator is surprisingly useful. It helps you find even and odd numbers, repeat patterns, and share things fairly.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

Seventeen sweets are shared between five children. Each child gets 3 sweets, and the remainder tells you how many are left. Also, any even number has a remainder of 0 when divided by 2:

Common mistakes

  • Using ^ for power. In JavaScript, 2 ^ 3 is a different operator and gives 1. Use 2 ** 3.
  • Forgetting the order of operations. Use brackets when you are not sure.
  • Thinking % means percent. It means remainder.
  • Dividing by zero does not crash the program. It gives Infinity.

Key points

  • + - * / work as you expect. % gives the remainder, and ** is "to the power of".
  • Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. Brackets go first.
  • number % 2 === 0 is a common way to test for an even number.
  • + also joins strings.

Practice

  1. Print the result of (8 + 2) * 5 and of 8 + 2 * 5. Why are they different?
  2. What is 25 % 4? Check with the console.
  3. Print the area of a square with side 9 using **.

4.2Assignment and Increment/Decrement Operators

What is it?

You already know =, which stores a value in a variable. Assignment shortcuts like += update a variable using its own old value. The increment ++ adds 1 and the decrement -- subtracts 1.

Why do we use it?

Updating a variable is so common that programmers made shortcuts for it. score += 5 is shorter and easier to read than score = score + 5. Counting up or down with ++ and -- is used everywhere.

Syntax

Simple example

++ before or after?

x++ gives the old value first and then adds 1. ++x adds 1 first and then gives the new value.

To stay safe, use x++ on its own line, and avoid mixing it into other expressions.

Real-world example

A game tracks the player's lives and coins:

Common mistakes

  • Writing x =+ 5 instead of x += 5. The first one just sets x to positive 5.
  • Using ++ or += on a const variable. It gives an error, because it changes the value.
  • Mixing x++ into bigger expressions, which makes code hard to understand.

Key points

  • +=, -=, *=, and /= update a variable using its old value.
  • ++ adds 1, and -- subtracts 1.
  • The variable must be created with let, not const.
  • Keep ++ and -- on their own line.

Practice

  1. Start with let count = 0. Use ++ three times and print the result.
  2. Start with let price = 100. Use *= to double it, then -= to take off 20.
  3. What are a and b after let a = 3; let b = a++;? Predict first, then run it.

4.3Comparison Operators

What is it?

Comparison operators compare two values and always give a boolean (true or false).

Operator Meaning
> and < Greater than, less than
>= and <= Greater than or equal, less than or equal
=== Strict equal: same value and same type
!== Strict not equal
== and != Loose equal and not equal (avoid them)

The loose == tries to change the types before it compares, which gives surprising results. 5 == "5" is true. The strict === does not change anything, so 5 === "5" is false.

Why do we use it?

Decisions depend on comparisons: Is the age at least 18? Does the password match? Is the score higher than the best score?

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A ticket machine checks age, and a lock checks a PIN. Notice how === catches a PIN that is stored as text:

Common mistakes

  • Using one = when you want to compare. = stores a value, and === compares.
  • Using == out of habit. Always write === and !==.
  • Trusting decimal comparisons: 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is false, because of tiny rounding errors.

Key points

  • Comparisons give true or false.
  • Use === and !==, and avoid == and !=.
  • === checks the value and the type.
  • One = stores, and three === compare.

Practice

  1. Print the result of 7 >= 7 and of 7 > 7.
  2. Predict, then check: "10" === 10 and "10" == 10.
  3. Store your age in a variable and print whether you are older than 13.

4.4Logical Operators

What is it?

Logical operators combine yes-or-no answers.

  • && (AND): true only if both sides are true.
  • || (OR): true if at least one side is true.
  • ! (NOT): flips true to false, and false to true.
A B A && B A || B
true true true true
true false false true
false true false true
false false false false

Why do we use it?

Real decisions have more than one condition: "The user is logged in and has paid", or "It is Saturday or Sunday".

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A cinema gives a discount to students or seniors, and a weekend check compares a day with two possible values:

Common mistakes

  • Using a single & or |. Those are different operators. Use && and ||.
  • Writing day === "Saturday" || "Sunday". Each side of || needs its own full comparison, as in the example above.
  • Forgetting brackets when mixing && and ||. && is done before ||, so add brackets to be clear.

Key points

  • && needs both sides true.
  • || needs at least one side true.
  • ! flips a boolean.
  • Each side of && and || should be a complete comparison.

Practice

  1. Write a condition that is true when age is between 13 and 19 (including both).
  2. What is !(5 > 3)? Predict, then check.
  3. Write a condition that is true if day is "Saturday" or "Sunday".

4.5The Ternary Operator

What is it?

The ternary operator is a one-line shortcut for choosing between two values. It is the only operator with three parts, which is why it is called "ternary".

Why do we use it?

It keeps small decisions short and neat, such as choosing a piece of text depending on a condition.

Syntax

Read it as: "If the condition is true, use the first value, otherwise use the second."

Simple example

Real-world example

A shopping site shows "1 new message" or "3 new messages", with the right grammar:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the : part. condition ? value alone is an error.
  • Chaining many ternaries together. It becomes very hard to read, so use if / else instead (Chapter 5).
  • Using it to run several actions. A ternary is for choosing a value.

Key points

  • condition ? a : b gives a when the condition is true, otherwise b.
  • It is a short form of a simple if / else.
  • Use it for small choices only.

Practice

  1. Use a ternary to store "Even" or "Odd" for the number 7.
  2. Use a ternary to print "Pass" when marks >= 40 and "Fail" otherwise.
  3. Rewrite the unread example for a value of 0, so it says "No new messages". (Hint: you may need two questions.)
Mini project: Shopping Bill Calculator

A shop applies a member discount, adds tax, and gives free delivery for big bills. This uses almost every operator from this chapter.

Challenge: change isMember to false and quantity to 1. Predict the new output before you run it. Then add a variable tip and use += to add it to total.

Chapter 4 in one minute
  • Arithmetic: + - * / % **. Modulus gives the remainder.
  • +=, -=, ++, and -- update a variable in a shorter way.
  • Compare with === and !==. Avoid ==.
  • &&, ||, and ! combine yes-or-no answers.
  • condition ? a : b chooses between two values.

5
Chapter 5

Conditions

Every day you make decisions: if it is raining, take an umbrella; otherwise, wear sunglasses. Programs make decisions in the same way. Conditions let your code choose different paths depending on the situation. This is where programs start to feel smart.

What you will learn

  • Run code only when a condition is true, using if and else
  • Check many options with else if
  • Put one decision inside another (nested conditions)
  • Choose between two values with the ternary operator
  • Match exact values with switch
  • Understand truthy and falsy values

5.1if and else

What is it?

An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is true. An optional else block runs when the condition is false. A block is the code between curly brackets { }.

Why do we use it?

Without conditions, a program would do exactly the same thing every time. With conditions, it can react: show a welcome or an error, allow or block, give a discount or not.

Syntax

The condition goes inside brackets, and it should give true or false.

Simple example

Real-world example

An age checker for tickets. A museum charges less for children under 12:

Common mistakes

  • Using one = instead of ===. In if (age = 18) you store 18 into age, and the condition is always true.
  • Adding a semicolon right after the condition: if (age > 18); This ends the if early, so the block below always runs.
  • Forgetting or mismatching curly brackets. Every { needs its }.

Key points

  • if runs a block only when the condition is true.
  • else is the "otherwise" part, and it is optional.
  • Use === to compare, never a single =.
  • Indent the code inside { } so that it is easy to read.

Practice

  1. Write an if / else that prints "Pass" if marks is 40 or more, and "Fail" otherwise.
  2. Write an if that prints "It is hot!" when temperature is above 30. Test it with 35 and with 20.
  3. Store true in isRaining. Print "Take an umbrella" or "Enjoy the sun" accordingly.

5.2else if

What is it?

With else if you can check several conditions, one after the other. JavaScript checks from top to bottom. The first condition that is true runs, and all the rest are skipped.

Why do we use it?

Many decisions have more than two outcomes: grades A, B, C, or D; hot, warm, or cold; small, medium, or large.

Syntax

Simple example

Since 28 is not above 35, JavaScript moves on. Since 28 is above 25, it prints "Warm" and skips everything after it.

Real-world example

A grade calculator. A school turns marks into grades:

Common mistakes

  • Putting the conditions in the wrong order. If marks >= 40 came first, then a score of 95 would get a "D", because that check is true and stops the chain.
  • Using separate if statements when you meant else if. Separate if statements are all checked, and several can run.
  • Forgetting the last else for the "none of the above" case.

Key points

  • else if lets you check many conditions in order.
  • Only the first true block runs.
  • The order of the conditions matters: go from the most specific to the most general.
  • End with else to catch everything else.

Practice

  1. Write a program that prints "Child" for age under 13, "Teenager" for 13 to 19, and "Adult" otherwise.
  2. Change the grade calculator to give "Excellent" for 90 or more, "Good" for 60 to 89, and "Try again" below that.
  3. Print "Positive", "Negative", or "Zero" for a number stored in a variable.

5.3Nested Conditions

What is it?

A nested condition is an if inside another if. It is like a door with a second door behind it: you only reach the second check if you pass the first.

Why do we use it?

Some decisions come in steps. First you check whether a user is logged in, and then you check what kind of user they are.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A login check. The program checks the username first, and only then the password:

A safer login message

Real websites usually say "Username or password is incorrect" and do not tell you which one was wrong. That way, an attacker cannot learn which usernames exist.

Common mistakes

  • Nesting too deeply. If your code goes four or five levels in, look for a simpler way.
  • Mixing up which } closes which block. Indent carefully.
  • Nesting when && would be simpler. if (isLoggedIn && isAdmin) is one check instead of two.

Key points

  • A nested condition is an if inside an if.
  • The inner check only runs when the outer one is true.
  • Use && when both conditions lead to the same result.
  • Keep nesting shallow so that your code stays readable.

Practice

  1. Write a nested condition: if hasTicket is true, then check age. Print "Enter" when age >= 12, otherwise "Too young". If there is no ticket, print "Buy a ticket".
  2. Rewrite the admin example using &&, so that it prints "Welcome, admin!" or "Access denied".
  3. Add a third check to the login example: an isBlocked variable that stops everything if it is true.

5.4The Ternary Operator for Decisions

What is it?

You met the ternary operator in Chapter 4. It is a one-line if / else that produces a value. Here you learn when to choose it.

Why do we use it?

It makes small decisions short and neat. Use it when you just need to pick one of two values. Use if / else when you need several lines of code in each branch.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A website button changes its label depending on whether you are logged in:

Common mistakes

  • Chaining three or more ternaries. It is very hard to read, so switch to else if.
  • Using a ternary to run several actions. It is meant to choose a value.
  • Forgetting the : else part. A ternary always needs both values.

Key points

  • A ternary is a compact if / else that gives a value.
  • Use it for simple, two-way choices.
  • Use if / else when the logic grows.

Practice

  1. Use a ternary to store "Weekend" or "Weekday" in a variable, depending on a boolean isWeekend.
  2. Print "Even" or "Odd" for a number, using % and a ternary.
  3. When is if / else a better choice than a ternary? Write one sentence.

5.5The switch Statement

What is it?

A switch statement compares one value against many exact options, called cases. Think of a vending machine keypad: press B2 and you get exactly the item in B2.

Why do we use it?

When you compare the same variable against many exact values (days, menu choices, commands), switch is cleaner than a long else if chain.

Syntax

break stops the switch after a match. default is like the final else.

Simple example

Real-world example

A tiny calculator picks the operation from a text command. You can also let several cases share one block by leaving out break on purpose:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting break. JavaScript then "falls through" and runs the next case as well:
  • Trying to use ranges such as case > 5. A switch only matches exact values, so use if / else if for ranges.
  • Forgetting default. Then nothing happens when no case matches.
  • Forgetting that switch uses strict comparison (===): the number 1 does not match the text "1".

Key points

  • switch compares one value against many exact cases.
  • End each case with break, unless you want to fall through on purpose.
  • default handles all the other values.
  • Use if / else if for ranges and complex conditions.

Practice

  1. Write a switch that turns numbers 1 to 3 into "Small", "Medium", and "Large", with "Unknown" as the default.
  2. Make a traffic light: "red" prints "Stop", "yellow" prints "Get ready", "green" prints "Go".
  3. Remove one break on purpose and see what changes.

5.6Truthy and Falsy Values

What is it?

When JavaScript needs a true or false (for example, inside if ( )), it turns any value into a boolean. Values that become false are falsy. Everything else is truthy.

The falsy values are: false, 0, "" (an empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. Every other value is truthy, including "0", "false", and [].

Why do we use it?

It lets you write short checks. if (name) means "if name has something in it". You will use it very often, especially with user input.

Syntax

Simple example

Boolean(value) shows you how JavaScript sees any value:

Real-world example

A form checks that the user typed a name. It also uses || to fill in a default, because || picks the first truthy value:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that 0 is falsy. A score of 0 is a real score, but if (score) treats it as "no score":
  • Thinking "false" (text) is falsy. It is a non-empty string, so it is truthy.
  • Thinking an empty array [] is falsy. It is truthy.

Key points

  • Falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN.
  • Everything else is truthy.
  • if (value) is a short way to check that a value exists.
  • Be careful with 0 and "", which can be valid values.

Practice

  1. Use Boolean() to test " " (a space), [], and NaN. Predict first.
  2. Write a check that prints "Empty" when a string variable has no text.
  3. Use || to give nickname the default value "Friend" when the variable is empty.
Mini project: Cinema Ticket Machine

Use if / else if, switch, and logical operators together. The price depends on age, the day, and whether the customer is a student.

Challenge: add a senior discount: customers aged 60 or over pay half of the final price. Then test with the ages 3, 9, 15, and 65.

Chapter 5 in one minute
  • if / else if / else chooses one path, and the first true condition wins.
  • Nested conditions put one decision inside another, so keep them shallow.
  • The ternary condition ? a : b is a short if / else for values.
  • switch matches exact values, and do not forget break.
  • Falsy values are false, 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else is truthy.

PreviousChapter 4 — OperatorsNextChapter 6 — Loops
6
Chapter 6

Loops

Imagine writing "I will not talk in class" one hundred times on a board. You would get tired quickly, but a computer would not. A loop repeats a block of code again and again, so you write the instructions once and the computer does the boring part. Loops are how programs count, search, add up, and process lists of things.

What you will learn

  • Repeat code a fixed number of times with for
  • Repeat code until something changes with while and do...while
  • Spot and avoid infinite loops
  • Stop a loop early with break and skip a step with continue
  • Go through the items of a list with for...of
  • Go through the keys of an object with for...in

6.1The for Loop

What is it?

A for loop repeats a block of code a set number of times. It keeps a counter, checks the counter each time, and changes the counter after every round. One round of a loop is called an iteration.

Why do we use it?

When you already know how many times something must happen (10 times, 100 times, once for every student), for is the neatest tool. It keeps the counting in one line.

Syntax

The three parts inside the brackets are separated by semicolons:

  • start runs once, before the loop begins (usually let i = 1).
  • condition is checked before every round. If it is true, the block runs. If it is false, the loop ends.
  • update runs after every round (usually i++).

Simple example

Here is what JavaScript does: it sets i to 1, checks i <= 5, runs the block, adds 1 to i, checks again, and so on. When i becomes 6, the condition is false and the loop stops.

Real-world example

A times table. A quiz app prints the table of 7 with one loop:

You can also put a loop inside another loop. The inner loop finishes all its rounds for every single round of the outer loop:

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one errors. Writing i <= 3 when you meant i < 3 (or the other way around) gives one round too many or too few. Count carefully.
  • Forgetting the update part (i++). The counter never changes, so the loop never ends.
  • Using const for the counter. for (const i = 0; ...; i++) fails, because i++ tries to change a constant. Use let.
  • Using commas instead of semicolons between the three parts.

Key points

  • A for loop has three parts: start, condition, update.
  • The condition is checked before every round.
  • Use it when you know how many rounds you need.
  • Use let for the counter, and be careful with < and <=.

Practice

  1. Print the numbers 1 to 10 with a for loop.
  2. Print the even numbers from 2 to 20. (Hint: change the update part to i += 2.)
  3. Print a countdown from 5 to 1, then print "Go!" after the loop. (Hint: use i--.)

6.2The while Loop

What is it?

A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition is true. It does not have a built-in counter. It only asks one question before each round: "Should I go again?"

Why do we use it?

Sometimes you do not know in advance how many rounds you need. You might repeat until a bank balance reaches a goal, until a number gets small enough, or until the user types the right answer.

Syntax

You must change something inside the block so that the condition eventually becomes false.

Simple example

Real-world example

A savings goal. You save 500 every month, and you want to buy a phone that costs 3200. How many months will it take? You do not know the answer beforehand, so while is perfect:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to change the variable in the condition, which creates an infinite loop (see 6.4).
  • Starting with a condition that is already false. Then the loop runs zero times.
  • Using = instead of === in the condition.

Key points

  • while repeats as long as its condition is true.
  • The condition is checked before each round.
  • Use it when you do not know how many rounds you need.
  • Always change something inside the loop that moves it toward the end.

Practice

  1. Use a while loop to print the numbers 1 to 5.
  2. Start with let n = 100; and keep halving it (n = n / 2) while n is greater than 1. Print n each time.
  3. Change the savings goal example to save 750 per month. How many months now?

6.3The do...while Loop

What is it?

A do...while loop is like while, but it checks the condition after the block runs. That means the block always runs at least once.

Why do we use it?

Some tasks must happen once before you can decide whether to repeat them. A menu must be shown before the user can choose to leave. A password box must appear before it can say "wrong password".

Syntax

Notice the semicolon at the very end.

Simple example

Compare the two loops when the condition is false from the start:

Real-world example

A PIN screen. The screen must ask at least once. We pretend that the user types the wrong PIN twice and then the right one:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the semicolon after while (condition).
  • Using do...while when the block should not run at all for some values. Then use while.
  • Forgetting to change the value that the condition checks.

Key points

  • do...while runs the block first and checks the condition afterwards.
  • The block always runs at least once.
  • Use it for "ask first, then decide" situations.

Practice

  1. Write a do...while loop that prints "Hello" three times using a counter.
  2. Make a do...while whose condition is false at the start. How many times does it run?
  3. In your own words: when would you pick do...while over while?

6.4Infinite Loops

What is it?

An infinite loop is a loop that never stops, because its condition never becomes false. The program keeps repeating forever and cannot do anything else.

Why do we use it?

You do not want infinite loops by accident, so you must be able to recognize them. In a browser they freeze the tab. In Node.js they run until you press Ctrl + C. A few programs, such as games and servers, run on purpose "for ever", but they always have a way to stop.

Syntax

There is no special syntax. An infinite loop is a normal loop with a mistake. Here are the two most common ones (do not run these):

Simple example

The fix for Mistake 1 is one line. Change the counter so the condition can become false:

Real-world example

A loading screen that never ends. Imagine a game that shows "Loading..." until the files arrive. If the code forgets to check the files, or the check can never become true, the player stares at the screen forever. Programmers protect against this by adding a safety limit:

If your browser freezes

If a page freezes because of an infinite loop, close that tab and open the page again. In a terminal running Node.js, press Ctrl + C. Before you run a loop, ask yourself: "What makes this stop?"

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting i++ (or i--) inside a while loop.
  • Counting in the wrong direction: for (let i = 10; i > 0; i++) counts up, so i > 0 is always true.
  • Making the exit condition impossible, such as waiting for a number to equal 5.5 while you add whole numbers.

Key points

  • An infinite loop never ends because its condition never becomes false.
  • Always know what will make your loop stop.
  • Check that the counter moves in the right direction.
  • A safety limit is a good habit for loops that wait for something.

Practice

  1. Find the bug: let x = 5; while (x > 0) { console.log(x); }. Then fix it.
  2. Find the bug: for (let i = 10; i >= 0; i++) { ... }. What should the update be?
  3. Write a while loop with a safety limit of 5 attempts.

6.5break and continue

What is it?

Two small keywords give you control inside a loop:

  • break ends the whole loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one.

Why do we use it?

break saves time when you have already found what you are looking for. continue lets you skip items that you do not want to handle, without wrapping everything in an if.

Syntax

Simple example

When i is 4, continue skips the print. When i is 7, break stops the loop, so 7 to 10 are never printed.

Real-world example

Finding the first match. A shop wants the first number from 1 upward whose square is bigger than 200. As soon as it finds it, it stops looking:

Skipping the weekend. Days 6 and 7 are Saturday and Sunday. We skip them with continue:

A loop that stops on purpose

while (true) looks like an infinite loop, but if it has a break inside, it is a safe way to say "keep going until I say stop". You will see this pattern in many programs.

Common mistakes

  • Using break outside of a loop (or a switch). It causes a syntax error.
  • Using continue in a while loop before the counter is updated. The counter never moves and the loop never ends.
  • Expecting break to stop an outer loop. It only leaves the innermost loop that contains it.

Key points

  • break leaves the loop completely.
  • continue skips to the next round.
  • Both are usually placed inside an if.
  • In nested loops, break only affects the loop it is in.

Practice

  1. Print 1 to 20, but stop when you reach a number divisible by 8.
  2. Print 1 to 15, but skip all multiples of 3.
  3. Find the first number from 1 upward that is divisible by both 6 and 8. Use break.

6.6for...of

What is it?

A for...of loop goes through the items of a list, one by one. You do not need a counter. JavaScript hands you each item in turn.

A list is called an array and is written with square brackets: ["red", "green", "blue"]. You will learn arrays properly in Chapter 8. For now, just know that it is a list of values. for...of also works on the letters of a string.

Why do we use it?

Most of the time, you want to do something with every item: print each name, add up each price, check each answer. for...of says exactly that, and there is no counter to get wrong.

Syntax

item is a new variable name of your choice. It holds one value per round.

Simple example

Real-world example

A shopping cart total. The prices of the items in a cart are added up:

Common mistakes

  • Using in instead of of. for...in gives you the positions (0, 1, 2), not the values.
  • Trying to use for...of on a plain object. It gives an error, because objects are not lists. Use for...in for objects (next section).
  • Changing the list while looping over it. That can skip items.

Key points

  • for...of visits every value in an array or string.
  • No counter is needed.
  • The loop variable holds one item per round.
  • Use const for the loop variable unless you need to change it.

Practice

  1. Make an array of five of your favourite foods and print each one with for...of.
  2. Loop through the string "hello" and print each letter in capitals. (Hint: letter.toUpperCase().)
  3. Add up the numbers in [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42] using for...of.

6.7for...in

What is it?

A for...in loop goes through the keys (names) of an object. An object stores information as key: value pairs inside curly brackets, like { name: "Asha", age: 15 }. Chapter 9 covers objects in full.

Why do we use it?

When you want to look at every piece of information inside an object, for...in gives you each key. Then you can use the key to get its value.

Syntax

Use square brackets object[key] to read the value, because key is a variable.

Simple example

Real-world example

A price list. A canteen keeps its prices in an object. The loop prints every item and also adds up the price of one of everything:

Common mistakes

  • Writing student.key instead of student[key]. The dot looks for a property literally named "key", so you get undefined.
  • Using for...in on an array. The keys of an array are text like "0" and "1", which can give surprising results:
  • Forgetting the difference: in gives keys, of gives values.
of vs in

of gives you the objects (the values in a list). in gives you the indexes or keys (the names). Use for...of for arrays and strings, and for...in for objects.

Key points

  • for...in goes through the keys of an object.
  • Use object[key] with square brackets to read each value.
  • Do not use it on arrays. Use for...of instead.

Practice

  1. Make an object about a book with title, author, and pages. Print every key and value.
  2. Make an object of three subjects and their marks. Add up all the marks with for...in.
  3. Explain in one sentence why student.key does not work inside the loop.
Mini project: Loop Playground

Three classic loop puzzles in one program: a star triangle (nested loops), FizzBuzz (for with conditions), and a sum with while.

Challenge: make the triangle upside down (5 stars first, then 4, and so on). Then change FizzBuzz to count up to 30.

Chapter 6 in one minute
  • for repeats with a counter: for (let i = 0; i < n; i++).
  • while repeats while a condition is true. do...while runs at least once.
  • Infinite loops never end. Always know what stops your loop.
  • break leaves the loop. continue skips to the next round.
  • for...of gives the values of a list. for...in gives the keys of an object.

Chapter 7

Functions

Think of a juice machine. You put in fruit, press a button, and out comes juice. You do not need to know how the machine works inside, and you can use it as many times as you like. A function is that machine for code. You write the steps once, give them a name, and run them whenever you need. Functions are the most important tool for keeping programs short, tidy, and easy to fix.

What you will learn

  • Create a function and call it
  • Pass information in with parameters and arguments
  • Get a result out with return
  • Understand local and global scope
  • Write function expressions and arrow functions
  • Use default parameters and rest parameters
  • Pass a function into another function (a callback)

7.1Function Declarations

What is it?

A function is a named block of code that does one job. Creating it is called declaring the function. Running it is called calling (or invoking) the function.

Why do we use it?

Without functions, you would copy and paste the same code again and again. If you later needed to fix something, you would have to fix it in every copy. With a function, you change it in one place.

Syntax

Function names follow the same rules as variable names, and they usually start with a verb: showMenu, calculateTotal, sayHello.

Simple example

Declaring the function does nothing by itself. The code only runs when you call it with sayHello().

Real-world example

A report header. A school program prints the same header at the top of every report:

Declarations can be called early

JavaScript reads function declarations before it runs the rest of the code. So you can call a declared function above the place where you wrote it:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the round brackets when calling. sayHello; does nothing, but sayHello(); runs the function.
  • Declaring a function and never calling it.
  • Misspelling the name when you call it. sayhello() is not the same as sayHello().
  • Giving a function a vague name like doStuff. A good name tells you what the function does.

Key points

  • A function is a reusable block of code with a name.
  • Declare it with function name() { } and call it with name().
  • Functions save you from repeating code.
  • Use clear verb names for your functions.

Practice

  1. Write a function showTitle that prints your favourite book title. Call it three times.
  2. Write a function printLine that prints 20 dashes (-). Use it to draw a line above and below a message.
  3. Declare a function and call it before its declaration. Does it work?

7.2Parameters and Arguments

What is it?

Functions become much more useful when they can receive information. A parameter is a variable name inside the function's brackets. An argument is the real value you give when you call the function.

Think of a parameter as an empty box with a label, and the argument as the thing you put in the box.

Why do we use it?

With parameters, one function can work with different data each time: greet any name, add any two numbers, calculate the area of any rectangle.

Syntax

The arguments are matched to the parameters by position: first with first, second with second.

Simple example

Real-world example

A rectangle area helper. A room-planning tool needs the area of many different rooms:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting an argument. The missing parameter becomes undefined:
  • Giving arguments in the wrong order. divide(2, 10) and divide(10, 2) give different answers.
  • Mixing up the two words. Parameters are in the definition. Arguments are in the call.

Key points

  • Parameters are the names inside the brackets when you declare a function.
  • Arguments are the values you pass when you call it.
  • They match by position.
  • A missing argument makes the parameter undefined.

Practice

  1. Write printSquare(n) that prints the square of n. Call it with 4 and 9.
  2. Write introduce(name, age) that prints "I am ..., and I am ... years old.".
  3. What does introduce(15, "Asha") print if you swap the arguments by mistake?

7.3The return Statement

What is it?

So far, our functions have only printed things. The return statement sends a value back to the place where the function was called. That value can be stored in a variable or used in another calculation.

Why do we use it?

Printing is only for people to read. A returned value can be used by the program itself: saved, checked, added, or passed to another function. Most real functions return something.

Syntax

When JavaScript reaches return, the function ends immediately.

Simple example

Real-world example

A price calculator. A shop calculates the final price after a discount, and the result is used in more than one place:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting return. The function gives back undefined:
  • Writing code after return. It never runs, because the function has already ended.
  • Using console.log when you needed return. Printing a value does not give it back.

Key points

  • return sends a value back to the caller.
  • The function stops as soon as it returns.
  • A function without return gives back undefined.
  • Return values let you store and reuse results.

Practice

  1. Write multiply(a, b) that returns the product. Print multiply(6, 7).
  2. Write isAdult(age) that returns true when age is 18 or more, and false otherwise.
  3. Write average(a, b, c) that returns the average of three numbers.

7.4Scope: Local and Global Variables

What is it?

Scope means "where a variable can be seen". A variable made inside a function is local: only that function can see it. A variable made outside all functions is global: everything can see it.

Why do we use it?

Local variables keep functions independent, so one function cannot accidentally break another. Scope is also the reason for many confusing errors, so it is worth understanding early.

Syntax

Simple example

The function can read school because it is global. But room lives only inside the function, so outside it does not exist. (typeof gives "undefined" for a name that does not exist, instead of an error.)

Real-world example

A game score. Several functions share one global score:

Common mistakes

  • Trying to use a local variable outside its function. It does not exist there.
  • Creating a local variable with the same name as a global one. The local one hides the global one inside the function:
  • Using too many global variables. Any function can change them, which makes bugs hard to find.
  • Forgetting that let and const also stay inside any block { }, such as an if or a loop.

Key points

  • Variables made inside a function are local to it.
  • Global variables can be seen everywhere.
  • A local variable with the same name hides the global one.
  • Prefer local variables and pass data in with parameters.

Practice

  1. Create a function with a local variable secret. Try to print secret outside the function using typeof.
  2. Write a global taxRate and a function addTax(price) that uses it.
  3. Why is it safer to pass data through parameters than to use many global variables?

7.5Function Expressions

What is it?

A function expression creates a function and stores it in a variable. In JavaScript, a function is a value, just like a number or a string, so you can put it in a variable.

Why do we use it?

It shows an important idea: functions can be stored, passed around, and returned. You will need this for callbacks (7.9) and for many browser tools later in this book.

Syntax

The function on the right has no name of its own, so it is called an anonymous function. Notice the semicolon at the end, because this is a normal const statement.

Simple example

Real-world example

A validator. A signup form has small checking functions stored in variables:

Common mistakes

  • Calling a function expression before it is created. Unlike declarations, expressions are not available early:
  • Forgetting the semicolon after the closing }. It usually still works, but it is a good habit.
  • Forgetting the brackets when calling: square is the function itself, square(9) runs it.

Key points

  • A function can be stored in a variable.
  • A function expression is not available before its line runs.
  • Function expressions are usually written with const.
  • Storing functions in variables makes it possible to pass them around.

Practice

  1. Write a function expression cube that returns a number multiplied by itself twice.
  2. Store a function in isEven that returns true for even numbers.
  3. What does console.log(square) (without brackets) show, compared with console.log(square(3))?

7.6Arrow Functions

What is it?

An arrow function is a shorter way to write a function expression. It uses an arrow => instead of the word function.

Why do we use it?

Modern JavaScript uses arrow functions everywhere, especially for short helper functions. Less typing means clearer code.

Syntax

Simple example

The same function written in three ways:

Real-world example

Small helpers for a shop:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting return when you use curly braces. With { }, you must write return yourself:
  • Writing => the wrong way round. It is an equals sign followed by a greater-than sign: =>.
  • Using empty brackets incorrectly. A function with no parameters needs (): () => "hello".

Key points

  • An arrow function is a short function expression: (a, b) => a + b.
  • Without curly braces, the value is returned automatically.
  • With curly braces, you must use return.
  • Use () when there are no parameters.

Practice

  1. Rewrite const square = function (n) { return n * n; }; as an arrow function.
  2. Write an arrow function isPositive that returns true for numbers above 0.
  3. Write an arrow function with two parameters that returns the larger of them (use a ternary).

7.7Default Parameters

What is it?

A default parameter gives a parameter a value to use when no argument is given (or when it is undefined).

Why do we use it?

Some values are usually the same, such as a shipping fee or a greeting. Defaults let callers skip them, and they also protect you from undefined surprises.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

An online store. Delivery costs 50 unless the caller says otherwise:

Common mistakes

  • Thinking that the default is used for every empty-looking value. It is used only when the argument is missing or undefined:
  • Putting the default parameter first and a normal one after it. Put default parameters at the end.
  • Forgetting that the default is only a fallback. Passing an argument replaces it.

Key points

  • A default parameter is written as name = value.
  • It is used when the argument is missing or undefined.
  • null, 0, and "" are real values, so they do not trigger the default.
  • Put default parameters last.

Practice

  1. Write power(base, exponent = 2) that returns base ** exponent. Call it with one and with two arguments.
  2. Write welcome(name, city = "Paris") that prints a message using both.
  3. What does show(false) print in the example above? Why?

7.8Rest Parameters

What is it?

A rest parameter collects any number of extra arguments into one array. You write it with three dots ... before the last parameter name.

Why do we use it?

Sometimes you do not know how many values will come: the sum of any number of prices, the average of any number of marks. A rest parameter lets one function handle them all.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

An average marks calculator. Students can have any number of subjects:

The same dots can also spread

When you put ... in a function call, it does the opposite job: it spreads an array into separate arguments. For example, sum(...[1, 2, 3]) works like sum(1, 2, 3). You will use this again in the array and Math chapters.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the rest parameter anywhere except last. function f(...items, last) is a syntax error.
  • Using more than one rest parameter in the same function.
  • Forgetting that ...numbers is an array. You can loop over it and use .length, but it is not a single number.

Key points

  • ...name collects the remaining arguments into an array.
  • It must be the last parameter.
  • It works with any number of arguments, even none.
  • Loop over it with for...of.

Practice

  1. Write maxOf(...numbers) that returns the biggest number using a loop.
  2. Write joinWords(...words) that returns all the words joined with a space between them. (Hint: start with "" and add.)
  3. What does average() return in the example above when no marks are given? Try it.

7.9Callback Functions

What is it?

A callback is a function that you pass into another function, so that the other function can call it later. Think of leaving your phone number at a shop: "Call me when my order is ready."

Why do we use it?

Callbacks let you say what to do without deciding when or how often it happens. The other function decides that. Callbacks are used for timers, button clicks, loading data, and looping over lists.

Syntax

Simple example

The function repeat does not know what the action is. It only knows when to call it.

Real-world example

A timer. setTimeout is a built-in function that takes a callback and a delay in milliseconds. After the delay, it calls your function:

The book line prints before the tea line, because JavaScript does not wait. It schedules the callback and moves on.

Common mistakes

  • Calling the function instead of passing it. Compare:
  • Forgetting that a callback is just a normal function. You can write it inline or give it a name and pass the name.
  • Expecting the code after setTimeout to wait. It does not.

Key points

  • A callback is a function passed to another function.
  • The other function decides when to run it.
  • Pass the function itself (sayHi), not its result (sayHi()).
  • Callbacks are used everywhere: timers, events, and array methods.

Practice

  1. Write runTwice(action) that calls action two times. Pass it a function that prints "Hi!".
  2. Use setTimeout to print "Time is up!" after 300 milliseconds.
  3. Write calculate(a, b, operation) where operation is a function. Call it with (x, y) => x + y and with (x, y) => x * y.

Chapter 7 in one minute
  • A function is a reusable block: declare it once, call it many times.
  • Parameters are the names in the definition. Arguments are the values you pass.
  • return sends a value back and ends the function.
  • Local variables live inside a function. Global variables live outside.
  • Arrow functions are short function expressions: (a, b) => a + b.
  • Default parameters give fallback values. Rest parameters collect extras into an array.
  • A callback is a function you pass to another function.
