Project 1

Mini Bank Account

You have learned variables, data types, operators, conditions, loops, and functions. Now you will use all of them in one program: a tiny bank that keeps a balance, accepts deposits, allows withdrawals, and refuses the ones that are not allowed. Build it slowly, one step at a time, and run the code after each step.

What you will learn

  • Plan a program before writing it
  • Keep a shared value in a global variable
  • Write small functions that each do one job
  • Use return values to report success or failure
  • Combine if, for...of, and functions in one program

Step 1: Plan the bank

Before you type any code, decide what the bank must do. Write it as a short list:

  1. It starts with a balance.
  2. A deposit adds money.
  3. A withdrawal removes money, but only if there is enough money.
  4. Every action prints a message, so we can follow what happens.
  5. We feed it a list of transactions: a positive number is a deposit, a negative number is a withdrawal, and 0 is an invalid entry.
Plan first

Professional programmers plan before they code. A five-line plan like this one saves you from getting lost halfway through.

Step 2: The balance and the deposit function

The balance is a global variable, because every function needs to see and change it. A failed-transaction counter goes next to it.

Step 3: The withdraw function

A withdrawal must be checked first. If the amount is bigger than the balance, we refuse. The function returns true or false, so the caller knows what happened.

Step 4: One function to handle any transaction

This function reads the number and decides what to do. It also returns true or false.

Notice withdraw(-amount). A withdrawal arrives as a negative number such as -200. The minus sign in front turns it into a positive 200 before we pass it on.

Step 5: Run a list of transactions

Finally, a for...of loop feeds every transaction into the bank and counts the failures.

The complete program

Put all the steps together in one file and run it:

Follow the numbers by hand: 1000 + 500 = 1500, minus 200 = 1300. The 5000 withdrawal is refused, and so is the 0. Then 1300 + 250 = 1550, and the last withdrawal takes everything.

Your turn: challenges

  1. Add interest. Write an arrow function addInterest(ratePercent) that adds interest to the balance and returns the interest earned.
  2. Add an overdraft. Let the customer go down to -500 before a withdrawal is refused.
  3. Add a fee. Charge 10 for every withdrawal (but not for deposits).
  4. Add a transfer. Write transfer(amount) that withdraws money and reports whether it worked.
  5. Change the data. Try a longer list of transactions with your own numbers, and predict the final balance before you run it.
Hint for challenge 1

The interest is balance * ratePercent / 100. Add it to the balance and return it:

What you practised
  • Planning a program in plain words before coding.
  • A global variable (balance) shared by several functions.
  • Small functions that each do one job, and return values that report success.
  • if checks to protect the program from bad input.
  • A for...of loop that processes a whole list.
PreviousChapter 7 — FunctionsNextChapter 8 — Arrays
8
Chapter 8

Arrays

A shopping list, a class register, the songs in a playlist: real life is full of lists. Until now, each variable held only one value. An array holds a whole list of values in one variable, in order. Arrays are one of the most used tools in JavaScript, and the array methods you will learn here (map, filter, reduce, and friends) will change the way you write code.

What you will learn

  • Create arrays and read items by their index
  • Add and remove items with push, pop, shift, and unshift
  • Copy and cut arrays with slice and splice
  • Search with includes and indexOf, and join items into text
  • Loop with forEach
  • Transform lists with map, filter, find, some, every, and reduce
  • Sort arrays correctly

8.1Creating Arrays and Using Indexes

What is it?

An array is an ordered list of values inside square brackets, separated by commas. Each value is called an element or item. Each item has a position number called an index, and counting starts at 0, not 1.

Why do we use it?

Without arrays you would need a separate variable for every item (student1, student2, student3, ...). With an array, you keep them together and can loop over them, search them, and sort them.

Syntax

Simple example

The last item is always at index length - 1. An array can also hold mixed types, such as ["Asha", 15, true], but most arrays hold one kind of value.

Real-world example

A playlist. A music app keeps song names in an array and shows the first song and the number of songs:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that counting starts at 0. In an array of 3 items, the indexes are 0, 1, and 2. There is no item at index 3.
  • Reading an index that does not exist. You get undefined, not an error.
  • Thinking that const makes the array frozen. const only stops you from putting a different array in the variable. You can still change the items inside.
  • Using typeof to check for an array. It says "object". Use Array.isArray() instead:

Key points

  • An array is an ordered list inside [ ].
  • The first item has index 0, and the last has index length - 1.
  • array.length tells you how many items there are.
  • You can change an item with array[index] = value.
  • Use Array.isArray() to check whether something is an array.

Practice

  1. Make an array of your five favourite foods. Print the first and the last one.
  2. Change the second item to something else, then print the whole array.
  3. What does console.log(fruits[fruits.length]) print? Why?

8.2Adding and Removing Items

What is it?

Four methods change the ends of an array:

Method What it does
push(x) adds x to the end
pop() removes the last item and gives it back
unshift(x) adds x to the start
shift() removes the first item and gives it back

A method is a function that belongs to a value. You write it after a dot: array.push(...).

Why do we use it?

Lists change over time: people join a queue, songs are added, tasks are finished. These four methods handle almost every everyday change.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A ticket queue. People join at the back (push), and the person at the front is served first (shift):

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up push (end) and unshift (start), or pop (end) and shift (start). Remember: push and pop work at the end, like a stack of plates.
  • Forgetting that these methods change the original array.
  • Expecting push to give back the array. It gives back the new length:
  • Using pop() on an empty array. It gives back undefined.

Key points

  • push and pop work at the end. unshift and shift work at the start.
  • pop and shift give back the removed item.
  • All four change the original array.
  • push and unshift give back the new length.

Practice

  1. Start with an empty array. Add three names with push, then remove the first one with shift.
  2. Add "urgent" to the very start of ["email", "call"].
  3. Use pop to remove the last item and print what was removed.

8.3Copying and Cutting: slice and splice

What is it?

These two look alike, but they behave very differently:

  • slice(start, end) makes a copy of a part of the array. It does not change the original. The item at end is not included.
  • splice(start, deleteCount, ...newItems) changes the original array. It can remove items, insert items, or replace items.

Memory trick: splice is like surgery (it changes the patient), and slice is like a photocopy.

Why do we use it?

slice is safe when you need a piece of a list but want to keep the whole list. splice is how you remove a cancelled order from the middle of a list or add an item at an exact position.

Syntax

Simple example

slice(-2) counts from the end and gives the last two items. The original array is untouched.

Now the same array with splice:

Real-world example

A shopping cart. The customer removes one item and the app adds a free gift in the middle:

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up slice and splice. Only splice changes the original.
  • Forgetting that the end index in slice is not included. slice(1, 3) gives the items at index 1 and 2.
  • Forgetting the second argument of splice. splice(1) removes everything from index 1 to the end.
  • Forgetting that splice gives back the removed items, not the changed array.

Key points

  • slice(start, end) copies a part and leaves the original alone.
  • splice(start, count, ...items) removes, inserts, or replaces in the original array.
  • The end index of slice is not included.
  • Negative numbers in slice count from the end.

Practice

  1. Use slice to get the middle three items of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
  2. Use splice to remove "Tuesday" from ["Mon", "Tuesday", "Wed"].
  3. Use splice to insert "Cherry" between "Apple" and "Mango" in ["Apple", "Mango"].

8.4Searching and Joining

What is it?

Three helpful tools:

  • includes(x) tells you true or false: is x in the array?
  • indexOf(x) gives the index of the first x, or -1 if it is not there.
  • join(separator) joins all the items into one string, with the separator between them.

Why do we use it?

Programs constantly ask "is this already in the list?" and "where is it?". Joining turns a list into readable text for the screen.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A username check and a tag list. A signup page checks whether a name is taken, and a blog shows its tags as one line:

Common mistakes

  • Using indexOf inside an if without comparing. The index 0 is falsy, and -1 is truthy, so the check is backwards:
  • Forgetting that searching is case-sensitive. "Asha" and "asha" are different.
  • Using indexOf when you only need a yes or no. Use includes.

Key points

  • includes answers yes or no.
  • indexOf gives the position, or -1 when the item is missing.
  • Compare with -1 (or use includes), never test the index directly.
  • join turns an array into a string.

Practice

  1. Check whether "Sunday" is in an array of weekday names. Print true or false.
  2. Find the index of "blue" in ["red", "blue", "green"].
  3. Join ["2026", "09", "20"] with "-" to make a date string.

8.5Looping with forEach

What is it?

forEach runs a function once for every item in the array. You give it a callback (Chapter 7), and it hands over each item, and optionally the item's index.

Why do we use it?

It is a tidy way to do something with every item: print it, show it on the page, or check it. There is no counter to manage.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A numbered menu. A restaurant shows its dishes with numbers starting from 1:

Common mistakes

  • Expecting forEach to give back a new array. It always gives back undefined. Use map when you need a new array.
  • Trying to stop it with break. That does not work inside forEach. Use a for...of loop if you may need to stop early.
  • Forgetting that the callback receives the item first and the index second.

Key points

  • forEach calls your function once for each item.
  • The callback receives (item, index).
  • It returns nothing (undefined).
  • Use for...of if you need break or continue.

Practice

  1. Use forEach to print every number of [3, 6, 9] multiplied by 2.
  2. Print "Item 1: ...", "Item 2: ..." for an array of three things.
  3. Use forEach and a variable outside the loop to add up all the numbers in [5, 10, 15].

8.6Transforming with map

What is it?

map creates a new array by running a function on every item. The new array has the same length as the old one, and the original is not changed. Think of a machine on a factory belt that changes every item that passes.

Why do we use it?

Very often you need a changed version of a list: prices with tax added, names in capital letters, temperatures in Fahrenheit. map does this in one line.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

Adding tax and formatting names. A shop adds 10% tax to every price, and a school writes names in capital letters:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting return when you use curly braces. Every item becomes undefined:
  • Using map just to print things. That is a job for forEach.
  • Forgetting to store the result. numbers.map(...) on its own changes nothing. Save it in a variable.

Key points

  • map returns a new array of the same length.
  • The original array stays the same.
  • The callback must return the new value for each item.
  • Use map to transform, and forEach to just do something.

Practice

  1. Use map to turn [1, 2, 3] into their squares.
  2. Turn ["a", "b", "c"] into ["a!", "b!", "c!"].
  3. Given prices in [100, 200, 300], create a new array where each price has a 20% discount.

8.7Selecting with filter and find

What is it?

  • filter creates a new array with only the items that pass a test. The test is a function that returns true (keep) or false (drop).
  • find gives back the first item that passes the test, or undefined when nothing passes.

Why do we use it?

Searching and selecting are everyday jobs: show only the products under a price, list only the students who passed, find the first empty seat.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A price filter. A shop shows only the items that fit a budget of 300:

Common mistakes

  • Expecting filter to give one item. It always gives an array, even when only one item matches or none do ([]).
  • Using = instead of === inside the test.
  • Forgetting that find returns undefined when nothing matches. Check for that before using the result.
  • Forgetting to return a true or false when using curly braces.

Key points

  • filter returns a new array with all the matching items.
  • find returns the first matching item, or undefined.
  • The test function should return true or false.
  • The original array is not changed.

Practice

  1. Keep only the even numbers of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
  2. From ["apple", "kiwi", "banana", "fig"], keep only the words with more than 4 letters.
  3. Use find to get the first number above 50 in [10, 60, 30, 90].

8.8Checking with some and every

What is it?

  • some gives true if at least one item passes the test.
  • every gives true only if all the items pass the test.

Why do we use it?

They answer yes-or-no questions about a whole list: "Did anyone fail?", "Is everything filled in?", "Is there any item in stock?".

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A form check. A signup form is valid only when every field has something typed in:

Common mistakes

  • Mixing them up. some = at least one. every = all of them.
  • Forgetting the empty-array case: every on an empty array is true (nothing failed), and some on an empty array is false:
  • Using filter and checking the length when some would be simpler and faster.

Key points

  • some asks "is there at least one?".
  • every asks "are they all?".
  • Both give true or false.
  • They stop early as soon as the answer is known.

Practice

  1. Check whether [3, 7, 10] contains at least one even number.
  2. Check whether all the numbers in [4, 8, 12] are even.
  3. What do you expect [1, 2, 3].every(n => n > 0) to give? Try it.

8.9Combining with reduce

What is it?

reduce goes through an array and combines all the items into one single value. It keeps a running result, called the accumulator, and updates it with every item. It starts from a value you choose.

Why do we use it?

Adding up a cart, finding the biggest number, counting things: all of these turn a whole list into one answer.

Syntax

The start value comes last, after the function.

Simple example

Step by step: sum starts at 0. Then 0 + 10 = 10, then 10 + 20 = 30, then 30 + 30 = 60.

Real-world example

A cart total and the highest price:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the start value. It can work for numbers, but it fails on an empty array:
  • Forgetting to return the new accumulator when you use curly braces.
  • Mixing up the order of the parameters. The accumulator always comes first, the item second.

Key points

  • reduce turns a whole array into a single value.
  • The callback receives (accumulator, item).
  • Always give a start value as the second argument.
  • The callback must return the new accumulator.

Practice

  1. Use reduce to add up [5, 10, 15, 20].
  2. Use reduce to multiply all the numbers in [1, 2, 3, 4] together. What start value should you use?
  3. Use reduce to count how many words in ["a", "bb", "ccc"] have more than one letter.

8.10Sorting Arrays

What is it?

sort puts the items of an array in order. reverse flips the order. Both change the original array.

By default, sort treats every item as text and sorts alphabetically. That is fine for words, but it goes wrong for numbers. To sort numbers properly, you give sort a compare function: (a, b) => a - b for small to big, and (a, b) => b - a for big to small.

Why do we use it?

Leaderboards, price lists, and name lists all need order.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A leaderboard. A game keeps the original score order but shows a sorted copy. slice() with no arguments makes a copy first:

Common mistakes

  • Sorting numbers without a compare function. They are sorted as text, so 10 comes before 9:
  • Forgetting that sort changes the original array. Copy it first with slice() if you need the original order.
  • Writing the compare function as a > b. It must return a number (negative, zero, or positive), so use a - b.
  • Expecting capital and small letters to sort together. Capital letters come before small letters.

Key points

  • sort() alone sorts as text.
  • For numbers, use sort((a, b) => a - b) or sort((a, b) => b - a).
  • sort and reverse change the original array.
  • Copy with slice() first if you want to keep the original.

Practice

  1. Sort ["mango", "apple", "banana"] alphabetically.
  2. Sort [30, 4, 100, 25] from biggest to smallest.
  3. Make a sorted copy of [3, 1, 2] and check that the original did not change.
Mini project: Class Marks Analyzer

A teacher has two arrays: student names and marks. Use forEach, reduce, filter, every, indexOf, and sort to build a report. (In Chapter 9, you will learn a neater way to keep this data together.)

Challenge: add a sixth student, find the lowest mark, and print the names of everyone who scored above the class average.

Chapter 8 in one minute
  • An array is an ordered list in [ ]. Indexes start at 0, and length counts the items.
  • push and pop work at the end. unshift and shift work at the start.
  • slice copies a part. splice changes the original.
  • includes says yes or no. indexOf gives a position or -1.
  • forEach does something for each item. map makes a new transformed array.
  • filter keeps matching items. find gives the first match.
  • some asks "at least one?". every asks "all of them?". reduce combines everything into one value.
  • sort needs (a, b) => a - b for numbers, and it changes the original array.

Chapter 9

Objects

An array is a list, but some things are not just a list of values. A student has a name, an age, a class, and marks. A product has a title, a price, and a stock count. An object groups all the information about one thing together, and gives every piece a name. Objects are everywhere in JavaScript: the page, the browser, and even console are objects.

What you will learn

  • Create objects and read their properties with dot and bracket notation
  • Change, add, delete, and check properties
  • Write methods (functions inside objects)
  • Understand what this means inside a method
  • Work with objects inside objects
  • Handle lists of objects with map, filter, find, and sort
  • Use Object.keys, Object.values, and Object.entries

9.1Creating Objects and Reading Properties

What is it?

An object stores information as key: value pairs inside curly brackets { }. Each pair is called a property. The key is the property's name, and the value can be anything: a number, a string, an array, even another object.

Why do we use it?

An object keeps everything about one thing in one place. Compare two loose variables, studentName and studentAge, with one object student. The object is easier to pass around and easier to understand.

Syntax

Properties are separated by commas. A colon : joins each key to its value.

Simple example

Dot notation is shorter and used most of the time. Bracket notation is needed when the key is stored in a variable, or when it has spaces:

Real-world example

A product in a shop. The shop shows its details on the screen:

Common mistakes

  • Using a semicolon or forgetting the comma between properties. Use commas.
  • Writing student.wanted when you mean the key stored in the variable wanted. Use student[wanted].
  • Reading a property that does not exist. You get undefined, not an error.
  • Forgetting the quotes on keys that have spaces or dashes. Those keys need "...", and bracket notation to read them.

Key points

  • An object is a collection of key: value properties in { }.
  • Read a property with object.key or object["key"].
  • Use brackets when the key is in a variable or has spaces.
  • A missing property gives undefined.

Practice

  1. Make an object book with title, author, and pages. Print each one.
  2. Store the text "pages" in a variable, and use it to read book.pages with brackets.
  3. Print book.publisher. What do you get, and why?

9.2Changing, Adding, and Deleting Properties

What is it?

Objects are not fixed. You can change a property by assigning a new value, add a property by assigning to a new key, and delete a property with the delete keyword. The in operator checks whether a property exists.

Why do we use it?

Information changes: a user gets older, changes their email, or removes a phone number. The object must be able to change with it.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

Updating a profile. A user changes their email and adds a phone number:

Common mistakes

  • Thinking const stops you from changing an object. It only stops you from replacing the whole object with a different one. The properties inside can change.
  • Making a typo. student.nmae = "Ravi" does not give an error. It quietly adds a new property called nmae.
  • Thinking that const copy = original makes a copy. Both names point to the same object:

The three dots { ...original } spread all the properties of original into a brand-new object, which is how you make a real copy.

Key points

  • Assign to a key to change or add a property.
  • delete object.key removes a property.
  • "key" in object checks that a key exists.
  • const objects can still change inside.
  • const b = a does not copy an object. Use { ...a }.

Practice

  1. Create car = { brand: "Toyota", year: 2015 }. Change the year, add a color, and print the object.
  2. Delete the brand and check with in that it is gone.
  3. Make a real copy of car with the spread dots, change the copy's color, and show that the original did not change.

9.3Methods

What is it?

A method is a function stored as a property of an object. It describes something the object can do. Properties are what an object has, and methods are what an object does.

Why do we use it?

Grouping actions with data keeps related code together. A dog object can have a name and also a bark action. You have already used methods without knowing: console.log(...) is the log method of the console object.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A small calculator object keeps its operations together:

Objects are everywhere

console is an object and log is its method. Math is an object too, and Math.round() is one of its methods. You will meet Math in Chapter 11. In Chapter 12, the whole web page becomes an object named document.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the brackets when calling a method. dog.bark is the function itself (not a call), and dog.bark() runs it:
  • Forgetting the comma between one method and the next one.
  • Writing dog.bark() when the method does not exist. That gives an error, because undefined is not a function.

Key points

  • A method is a function inside an object.
  • Write it as name() { ... } or name: function () { ... }.
  • Call it with brackets: object.method().
  • console.log and Math.round are methods too.

Practice

  1. Make an object robot with a method greet that prints "Beep boop!".
  2. Add a method add(a, b) to robot that returns the sum.
  3. Print robot.greet without brackets, then call it with brackets. What is the difference?

9.4The this Keyword

What is it?

Inside a method, this means "the object that this method belongs to". It lets a method read and change the object's own properties.

Why do we use it?

Without this, a method would have to hard-code the name of its object. With this, the same method works correctly for whichever object is using it.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A bank account object. The balance lives inside the object, and the methods use this to reach it:

Compare this with Project 1, where the balance was a global variable. Here, the data and the actions live together in one tidy object.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting this. in front of a property. Writing just balance inside the method looks for a normal variable, and gives an error.
  • Using an arrow function as a method. Arrow functions do not get their own this, so this.name will not find the object's name:

Use the hello() { ... } form for methods.

  • Thinking this always means the same thing. It depends on how the function is called. In a method call like person.introduce(), it is the object before the dot.

Key points

  • this inside a method is the object that owns the method.
  • Use this.property to read or change the object's own data.
  • Write methods with name() { }, not with arrow functions.

Practice

  1. Make a counter object with count: 0 and a method increment() that adds 1 to this.count. Call it three times and print the count.
  2. Add a reset() method to counter that sets the count back to 0.
  3. Explain in one sentence why an arrow function is a poor choice for an object method.

9.5Nested Objects

What is it?

A property's value can itself be an object. This is called a nested object. To reach the inner values, chain the dots: student.address.city.

Why do we use it?

Real information has layers. A student has an address, and the address has a city and a street. A nested object keeps those layers organised.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A user with settings. An app stores preferences inside the user object, and uses ?. (optional chaining) to read a value that might not exist:

The ?. operator means "if the thing before me exists, go on. Otherwise, stop and give undefined."

Common mistakes

  • Reading a value from something that does not exist. This is one of the most common errors in JavaScript:

user.contact is undefined, and you cannot look inside undefined. Use ?. or check first.

  • Losing track of the levels. Read from left to right: student.address.city means "the student, then the address, then the city".
  • Making objects nested more than two or three levels deep. It becomes hard to read.

Key points

  • A property can hold another object.
  • Chain the dots to go deeper: a.b.c.
  • ?. avoids errors when a middle part is missing.
  • Cannot read properties of undefined means an earlier step was undefined.

Practice

  1. Make a school object with a nested principal object (name and phone). Print the principal's name.
  2. Add a year property inside principal.
  3. Print school.library.books using ?. so that it does not crash.

9.6Arrays of Objects

What is it?

Real programs usually keep many objects in one array: a list of students, a list of products, a list of messages. All the array methods from Chapter 8 work on them.

Why do we use it?

This is the most common shape of data in real websites and apps. When you read a list from a server, it usually arrives as an array of objects.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A product list. A shop uses map, filter, find, reduce, and sort on its products:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the dot: p.price, not p. Each item in the array is a whole object.
  • Returning an object from an arrow function without extra brackets. JavaScript thinks { starts a block. Wrap the object in ( ):
  • Forgetting that find gives back the same object, not a copy. Changing it changes the array's object too.
  • Sorting objects without telling sort which property to compare.

Key points

  • An array of objects is the most common data shape.
  • Reach a value with list[index].key.
  • map, filter, find, reduce, and sort all work with objects.
  • Wrap an object in brackets when an arrow function returns it: x => ({ ... }).

Practice

  1. Make an array of three books (title and pages). Print the title of the last one.
  2. Use filter to keep the books with more than 200 pages.
  3. Use reduce to add up the pages of all the books.

9.7Object.keys, Object.values, and Object.entries

What is it?

Three built-in helpers turn an object into arrays, so you can use all the array tools on it:

  • Object.keys(obj) gives an array of the keys.
  • Object.values(obj) gives an array of the values.
  • Object.entries(obj) gives an array of [key, value] pairs.

Why do we use it?

You often need to count properties, add up all the values, or loop through everything in an object. These helpers make that easy and safer than for...in.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A report card. Add up the marks with values, and print every subject with entries. The [subject, mark] in the loop unpacks each pair into two variables (this is called destructuring):

See an object as text

JSON.stringify(object) turns an object into a single line of text. It is handy for looking inside an object: console.log(JSON.stringify({ name: "Asha", age: 15 })) prints {"name":"Asha","age":15}. You will meet JSON properly when you learn how programs share data.

Common mistakes

  • Using .length on an object. Objects have no length. Use Object.keys(obj).length.
  • Forgetting the capital O in Object.
  • Expecting Object.entries to give an object. It gives an array of pairs.

Key points

  • Object.keys gives the keys, Object.values the values, and Object.entries the pairs.
  • All three give arrays, so map, filter, reduce, and for...of work on them.
  • Count the properties with Object.keys(obj).length.

Practice

  1. Print all the keys of { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.
  2. Find the sum of the values of { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } using Object.values and reduce.
  3. Loop over Object.entries of a small prices object and print "item costs price" for each.
Mini project: Student Report Cards

Chapter 8's marks analyzer used two separate arrays. Now the data is tidier: each student is an object with a nested marks object. You will combine Object.values, Object.entries, map, sort, and filter.

Challenge: add a city property to each student. Then print the names of the students from one city. Finally, add a method describe() to each student that returns a sentence with the name and the average.

Chapter 9 in one minute
  • An object stores key: value properties inside { }.
  • Read with obj.key or obj["key"]. Change, add, and delete properties freely.
  • A method is a function inside an object. this is the object that owns the method.
  • Objects can be nested. Use ?. when a middle part might be missing.
  • An array of objects is the most common shape of real data.
  • Object.keys, Object.values, and Object.entries turn an object into arrays.
  • const b = a does not copy an object. Use { ...a }.

10
Chapter 10

Strings

Almost everything you see on a website is text: names, messages, titles, search words, passwords. In JavaScript, text is stored in strings, and strings come with a big toolbox of built-in methods. In this chapter you will learn how to measure text, clean it, search inside it, cut pieces out of it, and change it. These skills are used in nearly every real project.

What you will learn

  • Find the length of a string and read single characters
  • Write special characters with escape sequences and multi-line text
  • Change case and remove extra spaces
  • Search with includes, startsWith, endsWith, and indexOf
  • Cut out parts with slice and substring
  • Replace text with replace and replaceAll
  • Turn text into arrays and back with split and join

10.1String Length and Characters

What is it?

A string is a sequence of characters (letters, digits, spaces, and symbols). Like an array, each character has an index that starts at 0. The length property tells you how many characters the string has.

Why do we use it?

You need the length to check a password, limit a username, or find the last letter. Reading single characters lets you look at the first letter, or go through a word one letter at a time.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A username rule. A signup page accepts usernames that are 3 to 12 characters long:

Common mistakes

  • Writing word.length() with brackets. length is a property, not a method, so it has no brackets.
  • Forgetting that spaces count as characters. "a b" has a length of 3.
  • Forgetting that strings cannot be changed by index. The line below is ignored:

To get a different string, you must build a new one and store it.

Key points

  • string.length gives the number of characters (no brackets).
  • Characters have indexes starting at 0.
  • The last character is at index length - 1.
  • Strings cannot be changed in place. Methods return new strings.

Practice

  1. Print the length of your full name, including the space.
  2. Print the first and the last letter of the word "programming".
  3. Write a check that prints "Too short" when a password has fewer than 8 characters.

10.2Special Characters and Multi-line Text

What is it?

Some characters are hard to type inside quotes: a quote mark, a new line, or a backslash. You write them with an escape sequence: a backslash \ followed by a letter or symbol. Backticks (template literals) can also hold text over several lines.

Escape Meaning
\n new line
\t tab (a wide space)
\" a double quote
\' a single quote
\\ a backslash

Why do we use it?

Without escapes, a quote inside a string would end the string too early. Escapes also let you print messages over more than one line.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

An order message. Template literals keep line breaks exactly as you type them, and can hold values with ${ }:

Common mistakes

  • Using the same kind of quote inside the string without escaping it. This is a syntax error:

Use \", or choose a different outer quote, such as 'She said "Hello"'.

  • Writing /n (forward slash) instead of \n (backslash). The text /n is printed as it is.
  • Using a single backslash in a path: "C:\Users" does not work as you expect. Write "C:\\Users".

Key points

  • A backslash starts an escape sequence: \n, \t, \", \', \\.
  • \n makes a new line.
  • Backtick strings can span several lines and hold ${ } values.
  • To use a quote inside a string, escape it or use a different outer quote.

Practice

  1. Print He said "JavaScript is fun" with the double quotes included.
  2. Print three lines using a single string with \n.
  3. Write a multi-line greeting with backticks that includes your name in ${ }.

10.3Changing Case and Trimming

What is it?

  • toUpperCase() makes all letters capitals. toLowerCase() makes them all small.
  • trim() removes spaces (and new lines) from the start and end of a string. Spaces in the middle stay.

Why do we use it?

Users type in every way: ASHA, asha, Asha . To compare or store text properly, you first clean it into one standard form.

Syntax

Simple example

You can chain methods with dots. Each one works on the result of the one before it.

Real-world example

A login check. A user types their email with capital letters and extra spaces. The program cleans it before comparing:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that these methods return a new string and do not change the old one:
  • Expecting trim() to remove the spaces inside the text. It only cleans the two ends.
  • Forgetting the brackets: name.trim is the function itself, and name.trim() runs it.

Key points

  • toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() change the case.
  • trim() removes spaces from both ends.
  • Methods return a new string. Store it in a variable to keep it.
  • Chain methods: text.trim().toLowerCase().

Practice

  1. Turn "hello world" into "HELLO WORLD".
  2. Clean " Kiaan " so that it has no spaces, and print its length.
  3. Compare "YES" and "yes" in a way that treats them as equal.

10.4Searching Inside Strings

What is it?

Four methods look for text inside a string:

  • includes(text): does it contain this text? (true or false)
  • startsWith(text): does it begin with this text?
  • endsWith(text): does it end with this text?
  • indexOf(text): at which index does it first appear? (-1 if it does not.)

Why do we use it?

Searching is behind search boxes, spam filters, form checks, and file-type checks.

Syntax

Simple example

Notice that "script" (small s) is not found: searching is case-sensitive.

Real-world example

File types and a simple email check.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that searches are case-sensitive. Use toLowerCase() on both sides when case should not matter.
  • Testing indexOf directly in an if. The index 0 is falsy, and -1 is truthy. Compare with -1, or use includes.
  • Thinking that this simple email check is enough. Real email checking needs more rules.

Key points

  • includes, startsWith, and endsWith give true or false.
  • indexOf gives a position, or -1 when the text is missing.
  • All of them are case-sensitive.
  • Combine them with && and || for real checks.

Practice

  1. Check whether "I love coding" contains the word "love".
  2. Check whether a phone number string starts with "98".
  3. Find the position of the @ in "asha@example.com".

10.5Extracting Parts: slice and substring

What is it?

slice(start, end) copies a part of a string, from start up to (but not including) end. If you leave out end, it goes to the end of the string. substring(start, end) works almost the same way.

Why do we use it?

Cutting pieces out of text is how you get initials, the domain of an email address, the last digits of a number, or the first 100 letters of a long article.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

Initials, domain, and a hidden number.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that the end index is not included. slice(0, 4) gives 4 characters: indexes 0, 1, 2, and 3.
  • Forgetting the + 1 when you start after a found character, so the @ ends up in your result.
  • Using negative numbers with substring. It treats them as 0. Use slice for that.
  • Expecting the original string to change.

Key points

  • slice(start, end) copies a part. The end is not included.
  • slice(start) goes to the end. slice(-n) takes the last n characters.
  • Combine indexOf and slice to cut around a known character.
  • The original string is never changed.

Practice

  1. Print the first 3 letters of "Wednesday".
  2. Print the last 4 letters of "Wednesday".
  3. From "asha@example.com", print only the part before the @.

10.6Replacing Text

What is it?

  • replace(old, new) replaces the first match of old with new.
  • replaceAll(old, new) replaces every match.

Both give back a new string.

Why do we use it?

Cleaning and changing text is a daily job: hide bad words, turn spaces into dashes for a web address, or fix a spelling everywhere.

Syntax

Simple example

The middle word Cats (with a capital C) is not changed, because matching is case-sensitive.

Real-world example

A web address slug. A blog turns a title into a clean address, and a chat app hides a rude word:

Common mistakes

  • Using replace and expecting every match to change. Only the first one does. Use replaceAll.
  • Forgetting that the original string stays the same. Save the result.
  • Forgetting about capital letters. "Cats" and "cats" are different.

Key points

  • replace changes the first match. replaceAll changes every match.
  • Both return a new string.
  • Matching is case-sensitive.
  • Chain them with toLowerCase() and trim() to clean text.

Practice

  1. Replace "red" with "blue" in "red car, red bike", first with replace, then with replaceAll.
  2. Turn "2026-09-20" into "2026/09/20".
  3. Make a slug from "Learn JavaScript Fast".

10.7Splitting and Joining

What is it?

split(separator) cuts a string into pieces and gives you an array of the pieces. The separator is the text where you want to cut. join (from Chapter 8) does the opposite.

Why do we use it?

Data often arrives as one long string: a list separated by commas, a sentence made of words. Splitting lets you count, sort, and change the pieces. Then join puts them back together.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

Word count, title case, and a reversed word:

Three more handy tools

padStart fills the start of a string until it has a given length (good for clocks and dates). repeat copies a string many times. localeCompare sorts words correctly, even with mixed capital letters:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the separator. "a b".split() gives an array with the whole string inside: [ 'a b' ].
  • Splitting on a single space when there are double spaces. You get empty strings in the array:
  • Forgetting that the pieces are strings, even if they look like numbers. "15" + 1 is "151". Convert them first (Chapter 11).

Key points

  • split(separator) turns a string into an array.
  • split("") gives every character separately.
  • join(separator) turns an array back into a string.
  • The pieces from split are always strings.

Practice

  1. Split "red,green,blue" and print how many colours there are.
  2. Reverse the words (not the letters) of "one two three".
  3. Use split, map, and join to write every word of "hello big world" in capital letters.
Mini project: Text Toolkit

A tiny text analyzer that cleans a sentence and reports facts about it. It uses trim, split, map, slice, replaceAll, includes, and join together.

Challenge: add a check that tells you whether the text contains every letter of the alphabet (a "pangram"). Hint: loop over "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" and use includes.

Chapter 10 in one minute
  • length counts characters. string[0] reads one. Strings cannot be changed in place.
  • Escape sequences (\n, \", \\) write special characters. Backticks allow many lines.
  • toUpperCase, toLowerCase, and trim clean up text. They return new strings.
  • includes, startsWith, endsWith, and indexOf search. Searches are case-sensitive.
  • slice(start, end) cuts a part. The end index is not included.
  • replace changes the first match, replaceAll changes all of them.
  • split turns a string into an array, and join turns it back.

11
Chapter 11

Numbers and Math

Computers are great at maths, but JavaScript has a few surprises. Text from a form looks like a number but behaves like text. Some calculations give a strange result called NaN. Decimals are not always exact. In this chapter you will learn to convert text into numbers, catch bad numbers, round results, use the built-in Math object, and make random numbers for games and quizzes.

What you will learn

  • Convert text into numbers with Number, parseInt, and parseFloat
  • Understand NaN and check for it correctly
  • Round numbers with Math.round, Math.floor, Math.ceil, and Math.trunc
  • Use Math.max, Math.min, Math.abs, Math.sqrt, and Math.PI
  • Create random numbers and random choices
  • Format numbers with toFixed and toLocaleString, and understand why 0.1 + 0.2 is odd

11.1Converting Text to Numbers

What is it?

Whatever a user types into a page arrives as text, even when it looks like a number. To do maths with it, you must convert it. JavaScript gives you three tools:

  • Number(text) converts the whole text into a number.
  • parseInt(text) reads a whole number from the start of the text and ignores the rest.
  • parseFloat(text) reads a number with decimals from the start of the text.

Why do we use it?

Forms, prompts, and data files give you text. Without converting it, "10" + "20" becomes "1020", not 30.

Syntax

Simple example

Number is strict: any letters make the result NaN. parseInt and parseFloat are gentle: they read as many characters as they can, and stop at the first wrong one. Note that parseInt("3.99") gives 3. It cuts the decimals off, and does not round.

Real-world example

A form that adds two numbers. The two boxes give text, so the program must convert before adding:

Common mistakes

  • Adding text values with +. It joins them instead of adding them.
  • Forgetting that an empty string becomes 0, not an error:
  • Using parseInt when the number has decimals. It throws the decimals away.
  • Expecting -, *, and / to work like +. They convert text automatically ("6" * "2" is 12), but + does not. Convert on purpose so nothing is left to chance.

Key points

  • Input from users is always text. Convert it before doing maths.
  • Number(text) is strict. parseInt and parseFloat read from the start and stop at the first wrong character.
  • parseInt cuts off decimals. It does not round.
  • Number("") is 0, which can be a trap.

Practice

  1. Convert "250" into a number and add 50 to it.
  2. What do Number("12abc") and parseInt("12abc") give? Predict, then try.
  3. Use parseFloat to get the number out of "19.99 USD".

11.2NaN and Checking Numbers

What is it?

NaN means "Not a Number". You get it when a calculation cannot give a real number, for example Number("hello") or 0 / 0. Strangely, the type of NaN is "number", and NaN is not equal to anything, not even itself. To test for it, use Number.isNaN(value).

Why do we use it?

Bad input is normal: users type letters where numbers should be. If you do not catch NaN, it spreads through your calculations and ruins every result.

Syntax

Simple example

Dividing a number by zero does not crash. It gives Infinity. And NaN is contagious: any calculation with NaN gives NaN.

Real-world example

An age checker. It rejects text that is not a number, empty text, and impossible ages:

Common mistakes

  • Testing with value === NaN. It is always false. Use Number.isNaN(value).
  • Forgetting that empty input becomes 0, which passes as a number. Check for empty text first.
  • Using the old global isNaN("abc"). It converts its input first, which can surprise you. Number.isNaN is more precise.

Key points

  • NaN means the result is not a valid number.
  • NaN is not equal to anything, so use Number.isNaN() to test for it.
  • Any maths that involves NaN gives NaN.
  • Dividing by zero gives Infinity, not an error.

Practice

  1. Print the result of Number("12.5.3") and check it with Number.isNaN.
  2. Write isValidScore(text) that returns true only for numbers from 0 to 100.
  3. Explain in one sentence why NaN === NaN is false.

11.3Rounding Numbers

What is it?

The Math object gives you four ways to turn a decimal into a whole number:

Method What it does 4.3 4.7 -4.3
Math.round(x) nearest whole number 4 5 -4
Math.floor(x) always down 4 4 -5
Math.ceil(x) always up 5 5 -4
Math.trunc(x) cut off the decimals 4 4 -4

Why do we use it?

Prices, pages, boxes, and seats are whole things. You cannot sell 2.3 tickets or use 3.6 boxes. Rounding decides how to handle the extra part.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

Boxes and minutes. 10 friends need pizza, and one box feeds 4 people. How many boxes must you order? Also, how long is 125 seconds in minutes and seconds?

Here ceil is right, because 2.5 boxes means you need 3. And floor is right for minutes, because a minute is only counted once it is complete.

Common mistakes

  • Using floor when you need ceil, or the other way round. Ask: "Should the extra part count as a whole one?"
  • Forgetting how negative numbers behave. Math.floor(-4.1) is -5, and Math.round(-4.5) is -4. Use trunc to simply cut.
  • Trying to round to decimals with Math.round(2.567, 2). It ignores the second argument. Multiply, round, and divide instead:

Key points

  • round goes to the nearest, floor goes down, ceil goes up, and trunc cuts off the decimals.
  • For negative numbers, floor and trunc are different.
  • To round to 2 decimals: Math.round(x * 100) / 100.
  • Choose by asking what the extra part should mean.

Practice

  1. A bus holds 40 students. How many buses are needed for 135 students? (Use Math.ceil.)
  2. Round 7.456 to 2 decimal places using Math.round.
  3. Convert 3725 seconds into hours, minutes, and seconds using Math.floor and %.

11.4Useful Math Methods

What is it?

The Math object is a toolbox of maths helpers. It is not something you create. It is always there, ready to use.

Tool What it gives
Math.abs(x) the size of the number without its sign
Math.max(a, b, ...) the biggest value
Math.min(a, b, ...) the smallest value
Math.sqrt(x) the square root
Math.pow(x, y) or x ** y x to the power of y
Math.PI the number pi (3.14159...)

Why do we use it?

Distances, areas, discounts, scores, and limits all need these tools. They save you from writing them yourself.

Syntax

Simple example

Real-world example

A circle, a distance, and the best score.

The three dots ...scores spread the array into separate values, so Math.max(...scores) works like Math.max(72, 95, 38, 60).

Common mistakes

  • Passing an array directly: Math.max([1, 2, 3]) gives NaN. Spread it with Math.max(...array).
  • Forgetting the capital M in Math.
  • Writing Math.PI() with brackets. PI is a value, not a function.
  • Forgetting that Math.max() with no values gives -Infinity.

Key points

  • Math is a built-in toolbox. Do not create it, just use it.
  • max and min take separate values. Use ...array to spread an array.
  • Math.sqrt, Math.abs, and Math.PI cover many everyday needs.
  • x ** y is the same as Math.pow(x, y).

Practice

  1. Find the area of a circle with radius 7, rounded to 1 decimal place.
  2. Use Math.max and Math.min to find the highest and lowest of [14, 3, 27, 9].
  3. The temperature dropped from 5 to -3. Use Math.abs to print how many degrees it dropped.

11.5Random Numbers

What is it?

Math.random() gives a random decimal number from 0 up to (but never including) 1. By multiplying, adding, and rounding down, you can turn it into random whole numbers in any range.

Why do we use it?

Games roll dice, quizzes shuffle questions, apps pick a "winner", and tools make sample data. All of them need randomness.

Syntax

Simple example

A dice roll is a random whole number from 1 to 6. Your numbers will be different each time you run this:

Here is how it works: Math.random() * 6 gives a decimal from 0 to 5.99..., Math.floor turns it into 0 to 5, and + 1 shifts it to 1 to 6.

Real-world example

Reusable random helpers. A game needs random integers, and a quiz needs a random item from a list. The outputs below are random, so this code prints checks that must always be true:

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting Math.floor. You get decimals like 3.7215, not whole numbers.
  • Off-by-one errors. Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) gives 0 to 5. Add + 1 for a dice.
  • Using Math.round instead of Math.floor. The smallest and largest values then come up only half as often.
  • Using Math.random() for passwords or secret codes. It is fine for games, but it is not secure. Real security needs special tools built for the job.

Key points

  • Math.random() gives a decimal from 0 up to (not including) 1.
  • Math.floor(Math.random() * n) gives a whole number from 0 to n - 1.
  • For a range, use Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min.
  • Pick a random array item with a random index.

Practice

  1. Write coinFlip() that returns "heads" or "tails" with equal chances.
  2. Print a random number between 10 and 20 (both included).
  3. Pick a random name from an array of five names.

11.6Formatting Numbers and Decimal Surprises

What is it?

  • toFixed(n) gives a string with exactly n digits after the decimal point.
  • toLocaleString() writes a number the way people read it, with commas and even currency signs.

Why do we use it?

Money should show two decimals (5.50, not 5.5). Big numbers are easier to read with separators (1,234,567). Formatting makes numbers friendly.

Syntax

Simple example

Notice that plain toLocaleString adds the comma but does not add a missing zero. Give it minimumFractionDigits: 2 when you want two decimals every time.

Real-world example

The 0.1 + 0.2 surprise. Computers store decimals in binary, and many decimals cannot be stored exactly. So tiny errors appear:

This is not a JavaScript bug. Almost every programming language does it. For money, many programs store whole amounts (like cents or paisa) and divide only at the end. To compare decimals, check that they are close enough, as in the last line.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that toFixed returns a string. "3.14" + 1 gives "3.141". Convert back with Number(...) if you need to do more maths.
  • Calling toFixed on text. "3.14159".toFixed(2) is an error. Convert with Number first.
  • Expecting toFixed to be perfect at rounding halves. Because of the binary storage, (1.005).toFixed(2) gives "1.00", not "1.01".
  • Comparing decimals with === after calculations.

Key points

  • toFixed(n) gives a string with n decimals.
  • toLocaleString() adds separators and can format currency.
  • Decimals are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3.
  • Compare decimals with a small tolerance, and keep money in whole units when possible.

Practice

  1. Show the price 7 as "7.00".
  2. Format 9876543.21 with commas for "en-US".
  3. Write a check that says 0.1 * 3 and 0.3 are "close enough", using Math.abs.
Mini project: Bill Splitter and Dice Lab

Two small programs in one file. The first splits a restaurant bill, and it needs Number, rounding, and toFixed. The second rolls a die 600 times and counts how often each face comes up. The counts change every run, so we print facts that are always true.

Challenge: print how many times each face appeared, using counts.forEach. With 600 rolls, each face should show up about 100 times. Then change the tip to a variable that the user can set.

Chapter 11 in one minute
  • Text from forms must be converted: Number(text), parseInt(text), parseFloat(text).
  • NaN means "not a number". Check it with Number.isNaN(), never with ===.
  • round, floor, ceil, and trunc turn decimals into whole numbers in different ways.
  • Math.max, Math.min, Math.abs, Math.sqrt, and Math.PI are everyday helpers. Spread arrays with ....
  • Math.floor(Math.random() * n) gives 0 to n - 1.
  • toFixed(2) returns a string. toLocaleString() adds commas and currency signs.
  • Decimals are not always exact: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004.

Now you will build the heart of a small library system. It can list books, search them, lend and take back books, add new ones, and report statistics. This is the kind of data handling that real apps do all the time.

What you will learn

  1. Keep a list of books. Each book has an id, title, author, year, pages, and available.

Each book is an object, and the whole library is an array of these objects.

12
Chapter 12

The DOM

So far, your programs have printed text into a console. Now the fun begins: JavaScript can change the web page itself. It can rewrite a heading, fill a list, turn a word red, or build a whole table from data. The tool that makes this possible is the DOM. In this chapter you will learn to find elements on a page, and to change, create, and remove them.

What you will learn

  • Explain what the DOM is and how document gives you access to it
  • Select elements with getElementById, querySelector, and querySelectorAll
  • Change text and HTML with textContent and innerHTML
  • Read and change attributes and form values
  • Add, remove, and toggle CSS classes, and set inline styles
  • Create new elements and add them to the page, or remove them
How the live examples work

From here on, the examples are real web page pieces that run right inside the book. The dark box shows the code (press Copy to take it). The white box under it is the live result. Anything sent to console.log appears in a small dark console box at the bottom of the result. Press Reset to run the example again.

In your own files, put the code in an .html file, place the <script> just before </body>, and look in the browser's Console tab (press F12) for console.log messages.

12.1What Is the DOM?

What is it?

When a browser loads your HTML, it does not keep it as plain text. It builds a tree of objects in memory, and this tree is the DOM: the Document Object Model. Every tag becomes an object called an element. The whole tree hangs from one object named document.

JavaScript can read this tree and change it. When the tree changes, the browser updates the screen immediately.

Why do we use it?

Without the DOM, JavaScript could only calculate things in secret. The DOM is the bridge between your code and what the user sees. Every interactive feature on the web (menus, likes, live search, games) works by changing the DOM.

Syntax

Simple example

The script below asks the DOM about itself. Watch the console box:

Live result: try it here

The body has three elements: the heading, the paragraph, and the <script> itself.

Real-world example

A welcome banner built from data. A page starts with a placeholder heading, and the script fills in the real message. (You will learn getElementById and textContent in the next sections. For now, just watch what happens.)

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the DOM is your .html file. It is a live copy in memory. When JavaScript changes the DOM, the page changes, but your file on disk stays exactly as it was.
  • Trying to use document in Node.js. It belongs to the browser, so Node.js gives an error.
  • Forgetting the <script> tag. Your JavaScript must be inside <script>...</script> or loaded from a file with <script src="...">.

Key points

  • The DOM is a tree of objects that the browser builds from your HTML.
  • document is the doorway to the whole tree.
  • Changing the DOM changes what the user sees, but not your .html file.
  • The DOM belongs to the browser, not to JavaScript itself.

Practice

  1. Draw the DOM tree of a page that has a <h1>, and a <ul> with two <li> items.
  2. Use document.body.children.length in a page with three paragraphs. What number do you expect? (Remember the <script>.)
  3. Explain in one sentence why changing the DOM does not change the .html file.

12.2Selecting Elements

What is it?

Before you can change an element, you have to find it. This is called selecting. There are three main tools:

Tool What it gives you
document.getElementById("id") the one element with that id
document.querySelector("selector") the first element that matches a CSS selector
document.querySelectorAll("selector") all matching elements, as a list

The selectors are the same ones you know from CSS: #title for an id, .item for a class, li for a tag, ul li for a tag inside a tag.

Why do we use it?

Every DOM job starts with "find the element". Once you have it, you can read it, change it, move it, or remove it.

Syntax

Simple example

The heading, the first item, and the whole list of items are selected and reported:

Live result: try it here

querySelectorAll gives a NodeList. It looks like an array: it has length, numbers as indexes, forEach, and it works with for...of.

Real-world example

A cart total read from the page. The prices are written in the HTML, and JavaScript adds them up:

Live result: try it here

Remember from Chapter 11 that text must be converted with Number(...) before doing maths.

Common mistakes

  • Running the script before the element exists. The browser reads the page from top to bottom, so a script placed above the element cannot find it. It gets null, and using null causes an error:
Live result: try it here

The fix is to put the script after the element (usually just before </body>).

  • Writing a # in getElementById("#title"). That method wants just the id: "title". Only querySelector uses the CSS form "#title".
  • Forgetting the dot for classes in querySelector("item"). That looks for a <item> tag. Use ".item".
  • Expecting querySelector to give many elements. It gives only the first match. Use querySelectorAll for all of them.
  • Calling map or filter on a NodeList. It does not have them. Convert it to a real array first:

Key points

  • getElementById("id") finds one element by its id (no #).
  • querySelector("css") finds the first match. querySelectorAll("css") finds all matches.
  • A NodeList has length, indexes, and forEach. Use Array.from() to get array methods.
  • If nothing matches, you get null (or an empty list). Put your script after the HTML.

Practice

  1. Select the element with the id "logo" and print its textContent.
  2. Select all the <p> elements in a page and print how many there are.
  3. Use querySelector with a selector that finds the first <li> inside <ul id="menu">.

12.3Changing Text and HTML

What is it?

Two properties change what is inside an element:

  • textContent reads or sets the plain text. Any <tags> you put in are shown as ordinary characters.
  • innerHTML reads or sets the inner HTML. Tags you put in become real elements.

Why do we use it?

This is the most direct way to change what the user reads: update a score, show an error message, fill in a name, or write a whole new block of content.

Syntax

Simple example

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

A countdown timer. setInterval is a built-in function (like setTimeout from Chapter 7). It calls your callback again and again, every 1000 milliseconds. The script updates the heading every second, then stops the timer with clearInterval. Press Reset to watch it again:

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Putting user-typed text into innerHTML. Hidden code inside that text could run on your page. This is a real security problem called XSS. For text that comes from a user, always use textContent:
  • Expecting textContent to create tags. <b> is shown as the characters <b>. Use innerHTML (with safe content) or create the elements (12.6).
  • Changing the variable instead of the property. heading = "New" does nothing to the page. You must write heading.textContent = "New".
  • Using innerHTML += again and again in a loop. It is slow, and it rebuilds all the elements every time.

Key points

  • textContent sets or reads plain text. It is the safe default.
  • innerHTML sets or reads HTML. Use it only with content you wrote yourself.
  • Never put text from a user into innerHTML.
  • You change the property of the element (el.textContent), not the variable.

Practice

  1. Write <p id="status">Loading...</p> and change it to "Ready!" with JavaScript.
  2. Use innerHTML to show a sentence with one bold word.
  3. Explain why textContent is safer than innerHTML for text typed by a user.

12.4Attributes and Form Values

What is it?

An attribute is extra information inside a tag: href, src, id, class, type, disabled, and more. JavaScript can read and change them:

  • getAttribute("name") reads an attribute. setAttribute("name", value) sets it. removeAttribute("name") removes it.
  • Many attributes also work as properties: link.href, button.disabled, checkbox.checked.
  • For form fields, input.value is the text inside the field.
  • data- attributes are your own custom labels, such as data-price="250". Read them through element.dataset.price.

Why do we use it?

Attributes control where links go, whether a button works, and what a form field holds. data- attributes let you attach small pieces of information to elements.

Syntax

Simple example

Live result: try it here

The link now works, the box is filled in, and the button is switched off.

Real-world example

Totals from data- attributes. Each item carries its price in a data-price attribute. The script adds them up:

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that input.value is always text, even for number fields. Convert it with Number(...).
  • Trying to switch off a boolean attribute with setAttribute("disabled", false). The attribute still exists, so the button stays disabled. Use the property instead:
  • Using textContent to fill an input box. Use .value.
  • Forgetting that the class attribute has its own tools (classList, next section).

Key points

  • getAttribute, setAttribute, and removeAttribute work with any attribute.
  • Use properties for common ones: link.href, button.disabled, input.value.
  • input.value is always text.
  • data-price="250" is read with element.dataset.price.

Practice

  1. Change the href of a link to point to another website.
  2. Fill in an input with your name, and print its value with console.log.
  3. Add data-stock="5" to a list item and print the stock number as a real number.

12.5Classes and Styles

What is it?

Every element has a classList that lets you add, remove, and check CSS classes:

  • classList.add("name") and classList.remove("name")
  • classList.toggle("name") adds the class if it is missing, and removes it if it is there.
  • classList.contains("name") tells you true or false.

You can also set a style directly with element.style.property. CSS names with a dash are written in camelCase: background-color becomes backgroundColor.

Why do we use it?

The best way to change how something looks is to write the styles in CSS once, and let JavaScript switch the classes on and off. Your design stays in your CSS, and your behaviour stays in JavaScript.

Syntax

Simple example

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

Order status badges. One function puts the right class on a badge, after removing the old ones:

Live result: try it here
toggle with a switch

classList.toggle("on", true) always adds the class, and classList.toggle("on", false) always removes it. So element.classList.toggle("on", someCondition) turns a class on or off to match a true or false value. You will use this in Chapter 13.

Common mistakes

  • Writing the dot in the class name: classList.add(".done"). Use just "done".
  • Using element.className = "done". It replaces every class the element already had. classList.add keeps the others.
  • Writing CSS names with a dash: element.style.background-color is a syntax error. Use backgroundColor.
  • Forgetting the unit: style.fontSize = 24 does nothing. Write "24px".
  • Expecting element.style to show styles that come from a CSS file. It shows only inline styles that you have set.

Key points

  • classList has add, remove, toggle, and contains.
  • Prefer switching classes over setting many styles in JavaScript.
  • style properties use camelCase, and values are text with units.
  • toggle(name, condition) turns a class on or off to match the condition.

Practice

  1. Add the class "highlight" to a paragraph, and define .highlight in CSS.
  2. Make a heading blue and 40px large using style.
  3. Use classList.contains to print whether an element has the class "done".

12.6Creating, Adding, and Removing Elements

What is it?

You can build new elements from nothing:

  • document.createElement("tag") makes a new, empty element. It is not on the page yet.
  • parent.append(child) puts it at the end of the parent (and parent.prepend(child) puts it at the start).
  • element.remove() takes an element off the page.

Why do we use it?

Real pages are built from data: a list of products, a table of students, a feed of messages. You write the pattern once, and JavaScript creates as many elements as the data needs.

Syntax

Simple example

A list is built from an array:

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

A results table from data. Every student in the array becomes a table row. Failing marks get a red class:

Live result: try it here

To remove an element, select it and call remove(). To empty a whole container, set container.innerHTML = "":

Common mistakes

  • Creating an element and forgetting to add it. Until you call append, it exists only in memory, and nobody can see it.
  • Forgetting document. in front of createElement.
  • Adding the same element twice and expecting two copies. An element can only be in one place, so it moves. Create a new element each time (for example, inside the loop).
  • Building HTML by joining strings with user text. Create elements and use textContent.
  • Confusing append and appendChild. append is newer and more flexible: it takes several items, and text too.

Key points

  • createElement makes an element, append puts it on the page, and remove takes it away.
  • Create a new element for every item.
  • Use textContent to fill elements with text.
  • Loop over an array of data to build lists and tables.

Practice

  1. Make an empty <ul id="days"> and fill it with the seven days of the week from an array.
  2. Create a <p>, give it a class, put text in it, and add it to the <body>.
  3. Add a "Delete" step: use remove() to delete the first <li> of a list.

Chapter 12 in one minute
  • The DOM is a live tree of objects that the browser builds from your HTML. document is the doorway.
  • Select with getElementById, querySelector (first), and querySelectorAll (all).
  • Change text with textContent (safe) or HTML with innerHTML (only for your own content).
  • Attributes: setAttribute, properties like input.value and button.disabled, and dataset for data- attributes.
  • Style with classList (add, remove, toggle, contains), and style in camelCase.
  • Create with createElement, add with append, and take away with remove.
  • Place your script after the HTML, or the elements will not be found.
