Chapter 13

Events

A page that only changes by itself is not very interesting. A page that reacts to you is. When you click a button, type in a box, press a key, or move the mouse, the browser announces it. That announcement is called an event. In this chapter you will learn to listen for events and run your code when they happen. This is the step that turns a web page into a real application.

What you will learn

  • Listen for events with addEventListener
  • Use the event object (event.target, event.key, and more)
  • React to typing and choices with input and change
  • Handle form submission and stop the page from reloading
  • Respond to keyboard and mouse events
  • Use one listener for many elements (event delegation)

13.1Events and addEventListener

What is it?

An event is something that happens on the page: a click, a key press, a change in a text box, the page finishing loading. An event listener is a function that waits for one kind of event on one element, and runs when it happens.

You attach a listener with addEventListener. It takes two things: the name of the event (as text) and a callback function (Chapter 7) to run.

Why do we use it?

Without events, your code would run once at the start and then stop. Events let the user be in control: nothing happens until they click, type, or press something.

Syntax

Simple example

A button counts its own clicks:

Live result: try it here

The callback does not run when the page loads. It runs later, on every click.

Real-world example

A like button. It remembers whether you liked the post, changes its text, and switches a CSS class on and off:

Live result: try it here

The function draw() shows the current state on the screen. The listener changes the state and calls draw(). This "change the data, then redraw" pattern is used in almost every interactive app.

Common mistakes

  • Calling the function instead of passing it. This is the same mistake as with callbacks in Chapter 7:
  • Writing "onclick" as the event name. The name is just "click". (Other names are "input", "keydown", "submit", and so on.)
  • Misspelling the event name. "clik" gives no error. It just never fires.
  • Adding the same listener many times (for example, inside another listener). Then one click runs your code many times.
  • Selecting the element before it exists (see Chapter 12). Place your script after the HTML.

Key points

  • An event is something that happens. A listener is a function that waits for it.
  • element.addEventListener("eventName", callback) attaches one.
  • The callback runs later, every time the event happens.
  • Pass the function itself, without brackets.
  • Keep the data in variables, and write a function that redraws the screen from that data.

Practice

  1. Make a button that changes the text of a heading when clicked.
  2. Make a button that hides and shows a paragraph each time you click it. (Hint: add a CSS class .hidden { display: none; } and use classList.toggle.)
  3. Explain the difference between addEventListener("click", showMessage) and addEventListener("click", showMessage()).

13.2The Event Object

What is it?

When an event happens, the browser hands your callback an event object with details about what happened. You receive it as a parameter. Most people name it event (or e).

Property What it tells you
event.type the kind of event, such as "click"
event.target the exact element that was clicked (or typed in)
event.clientX, event.clientY mouse position in the window
event.offsetX, event.offsetY mouse position inside the element
event.key which key was pressed (for keyboard events)
event.preventDefault() stops the browser's normal action

Why do we use it?

Often you need to know which element was clicked, where the mouse was, or which key was pressed. The event object answers all of these.

Syntax

Simple example

One listener sits on the blue box. Click the buttons and the paragraph, and it reports which element you actually hit:

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

A click position tracker. Games and drawing tools need to know exactly where the user clicked:

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to write the parameter. function () { event.target } does not receive the event object, so it fails or uses an outdated global.
  • Confusing event.target (the element that was actually clicked, which might be a child) with event.currentTarget (the element that has the listener).
  • Using this inside an arrow function callback. Use event.currentTarget instead.
  • Thinking the parameter must be called event. Any name works, but event or e are standard.

Key points

  • The callback receives an event object as its first parameter.
  • event.target is the element that triggered the event.
  • event.offsetX and event.offsetY give the position inside the element.
  • event.preventDefault() stops the default browser action.

Practice

  1. Print event.type in the console when you click a button.
  2. Show the text of the clicked element with event.target.textContent.
  3. Find the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget by clicking a <span> inside a <button> that has the listener.

13.3Input and Change Events

What is it?

Two events tell you that the user changed a form field:

  • input fires every time the value changes, even by a single letter.
  • change fires when the user finishes a change: they leave a text box, pick an option, or tick a box.

Inside the handler, read the field's current value with input.value (or checkbox.checked for a tick box).

Why do we use it?

Live features like search-as-you-type, character counters, instant previews, and "agree" boxes all depend on these two events.

Syntax

Simple example

A greeting and a character counter that update with every key you type:

Live result: try it here

Here is change with a dropdown list and a check box:

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

Search as you type. Every letter you type filters the list. Each item is hidden if it does not contain the search word. The hidden property hides an element completely:

Live result: try it here

This uses string methods from Chapter 10: trim, toLowerCase, and includes.

Common mistakes

  • Reading input.value once, outside the handler. It gives the value from the moment the page loaded. Read it inside the handler.
  • Using change when you need instant updates. On a text box, change waits until the user leaves the box. Use input.
  • Forgetting that value is always text. Convert numbers with Number(...).
  • Forgetting trim() and toLowerCase() when searching. "Apple" and "apple " are not equal.
  • Using keyup to track typing. It misses pasting with the mouse. Use input.

Key points

  • input fires on every change. change fires when a choice is finished.
  • Read the current value inside the handler with .value (or .checked for check boxes).
  • value is always text.
  • Clean the text with trim() and toLowerCase() before comparing.

Practice

  1. Show what the user types in a text box, live, inside a <p>.
  2. Make a select box of three cities that shows the chosen city in a <p>.
  3. Make a check box that shows or hides a paragraph.

13.4Forms and the submit Event

What is it?

A <form> fires a submit event when the user presses its submit button or presses Enter inside a field. Normally the browser then sends the form away and reloads the page. To handle the form yourself, call event.preventDefault() at the start of the handler.

Why do we use it?

Forms are the main way that users give information to a website. Listening for submit lets you check the values, show messages, and add the new data to the page, all without a reload.

Syntax

Simple example

A signup form with two checks:

Live result: try it here

Try it: press Enter inside a box, or click Join. Both fire the same submit event.

Real-world example

A guest book. Each message is added to the top of a list. The text goes in with textContent, so anything a visitor types is shown safely. After adding, form.reset() clears the boxes:

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting event.preventDefault(). The browser reloads the page, and all your work disappears.
  • Listening for click on the submit button instead of submit on the form. Then pressing Enter does not work.
  • Not checking the input before using it. Empty boxes, spaces only, and text where you expected numbers are all normal.
  • Building the new content with innerHTML and the visitor's text. Use createElement and textContent.

Key points

  • A form fires submit on the button and on the Enter key.
  • Call event.preventDefault() first to stop the reload.
  • Listen for submit on the form, not for click on the button.
  • Always check and clean input (trim, Number, length checks) before using it.
  • form.reset() clears the fields.

Practice

  1. Make a form with one number box. When submitted, show the number doubled in a paragraph.
  2. Add a check: show "Please type a number." when the box is empty or not a number.
  3. Add a "message board" like the guest book, but with a single text box.

13.5Keyboard Events

What is it?

Two events report key presses:

  • keydown fires when a key goes down (and repeats while it is held).
  • keyup fires when the key is released.

Inside the handler, event.key tells you which key: "a", "A", "Enter", "Escape", "ArrowLeft", " " (the space bar), and so on. You can listen on a single element, or on the whole document.

Why do we use it?

Games use the arrow keys. Apps use shortcuts such as Escape to close a window, or Enter to send a message.

Syntax

Simple example

Use the arrow keys to move the blue square. Press Enter to reset it. Click inside the box first, so the keyboard input goes to this example. Math.max and Math.min (Chapter 11) keep the square inside its stage:

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

Press Enter to add. A quick-add box for tasks, without a form:

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Comparing with the wrong text. event.key is case-sensitive: "Enter" works, "enter" does not, and "a" and "A" are different.
  • Using event.keyCode. It is old and deprecated. Use event.key.
  • Expecting keydown to give the finished text. To read what was typed in a box, use the input event.
  • Forgetting that a held key keeps firing keydown. You can check event.repeat.
  • Forgetting that the page must have keyboard focus. Click on it first.

Key points

  • keydown fires when a key goes down, and keyup when it is released.
  • event.key says which key: "Enter", "Escape", "ArrowLeft", "a", and so on.
  • Listen on document for keys anywhere on the page, or on one input for keys inside it.
  • Use event.preventDefault() to stop default actions such as scrolling.

Practice

  1. Print every key the user presses with console.log(event.key).
  2. Show a message "Escape pressed!" only when the Escape key is pressed.
  3. Make a text box that turns red when the user presses Enter while it is empty.

13.6Mouse Events

What is it?

Besides click, elements can react to many mouse events:

Event When it fires
dblclick the element is double-clicked
mouseenter the pointer moves onto the element
mouseleave the pointer moves off the element
mousemove the pointer moves while it is over the element
mousedown, mouseup a mouse button goes down, or comes back up
contextmenu the right mouse button is clicked

Why do we use it?

Hover effects, tooltips, drag and drop, and drawing tools all use mouse events.

Syntax

Simple example

Move the mouse onto the card and off again, and double-click it:

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

A live coordinates display. The numbers change every time the mouse moves inside the green box:

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Using mouseover and mouseout for hover effects on elements with children. Those events also fire when the pointer moves between the element and its children, which causes flicker. mouseenter and mouseleave do not.
  • Doing heavy work in mousemove. It fires many times per second, so keep the handler small.
  • Forgetting that phones and tablets have no hover. Important actions should also work with click.
  • Forgetting that offsetX is relative to the element, and clientX is relative to the window.

Key points

  • mouseenter and mouseleave are the best pair for hover effects.
  • mousemove reports the pointer position through the event object.
  • dblclick handles double-clicks.
  • Keep mousemove handlers short, and do not rely on hover alone.

Practice

  1. Make a box that turns green when the mouse enters and back to white when it leaves.
  2. Show "Ouch!" when a paragraph is double-clicked.
  3. Print the mouse position (clientX and clientY) when a button is right-clicked. (Hint: use contextmenu, and call preventDefault() to skip the browser menu.)

13.7Events on Many Elements: Delegation

What is it?

When you click a child element, the event does not stop there. It bubbles up: the parent hears it, then the parent's parent, all the way to the top of the page. This lets you put one listener on a parent, and use event.target to find out which child was clicked. This technique is called event delegation.

Two helpful tools:

  • element.closest("selector") finds the nearest parent (or the element itself) that matches the selector.
  • element.matches("selector") tells you true or false whether the element matches.

Why do we use it?

Real lists change: items are added and removed. If you attach a listener to every item, new items have none, and you need lots of listeners. A single listener on the parent handles all the current and future children.

Syntax

Simple example

Click an item to cross it out. Press Add item and try the new item too. It works with no extra code:

Live result: try it here

Real-world example

Many buttons, one listener. A keypad with ten buttons needs only one listener. Each button carries its digit in a data- attribute:

Live result: try it here

Common mistakes

  • Adding a listener to each new element by hand, or forgetting to add it to new ones. Use delegation for lists that change.
  • Using event.target directly when the item contains other tags. Clicking a <b> inside an <li> makes target the <b>. Use event.target.closest("li").
  • Forgetting the check for clicks on empty space. When the click is on the list itself (not on an item), closest gives null, so test for it.
  • Expecting every event to bubble. focus, blur, and mouseenter do not. (Use focusin, focusout, or mouseover when you need delegation.)

Key points

  • Events bubble from the clicked element up through its parents.
  • One listener on a parent can serve many children, even ones added later.
  • event.target.closest("selector") finds the item that was clicked.
  • Always check for null in case the click missed every item.

Practice

  1. Put one listener on a <ul> that shows the text of whichever <li> is clicked.
  2. Add a "Delete" button inside each <li>, and make it remove that <li> using delegation and matches.
  3. Explain in one sentence why delegation works for elements created after the listener was added.

Chapter 13 in one minute
  • An event is something that happens. element.addEventListener("click", callback) runs your function when it does.
  • Pass the function (handler), do not call it (handler()).
  • The callback receives an event object: event.target, event.key, event.offsetX, event.preventDefault().
  • input fires on every change. change fires when a choice is finished.
  • Listen for submit on the form, and call event.preventDefault() to stop the reload.
  • keydown and event.key handle the keyboard. mouseenter, mouseleave, and mousemove handle the mouse.
  • Events bubble. One listener on a parent plus event.target.closest(...) handles many children.
  • Keep your data in variables, and redraw the screen from that data.

Project 3

To-Do List App

This is the biggest project of the book so far, and a real application. You will build a to-do list that lets you add tasks, tick them off, delete them, filter them, and see how many are left. It uses everything from Part 3: selecting elements, creating elements, classes, events, forms, and event delegation. It also uses the arrays and objects of Part 2 to keep the data.

What you will learn

  • Keep an app's data in an array of objects
  • Write a render() function that redraws the screen from the data
  • Handle a form with submit
  • Use event delegation for buttons that are created later
  • Combine classes, data- attributes, and events in one working app

Step 1: Plan the app

Write down what the app must do:

  1. Show a list of tasks. Each task has a text, and can be done or not.
  2. A form adds a new task (and ignores empty ones).
  3. Clicking a task's text ticks it off, or un-ticks it. A small × button deletes it.
  4. A counter shows how many tasks are left (not done).
  5. Three filter buttons show All, Active, or Done tasks.
The most important idea: data first, screen second

Do not change the page directly when something happens. Instead, change the data (the tasks array), and then call one function, render(), that redraws the whole list from the data. The screen is always a picture of the data, so the two can never disagree. Most modern web apps are built on this idea.

Step 2: The HTML

The page needs a heading, a form, an empty list to fill, a message for an empty list, and a bar with the counter and the filter buttons. Notice that the list is empty, because JavaScript will build the items.

Step 3: The data and render()

The tasks live in an array of objects. Each object has an id (so we can tell tasks apart), the text, and a done flag. The variable filter remembers which filter is active.

render() is the heart of the app. It empties the list, builds one <li> for every visible task, and updates the counter, the empty message, and the filter buttons. The data-id attribute stores each task's id on its <li>, so a click can later tell which task it belongs to.

Step 4: Adding tasks

The form's submit event stops the page reload, cleans the text, ignores empty text, adds a new object to the array, clears the box, and redraws.

Step 5: Completing and deleting tasks

There is one listener on the <ul>. It finds which <li> was clicked, reads its id from data-id, and then either deletes that task (if the click was on the ×) or flips its done flag. Because we use delegation, new tasks work automatically.

Step 6: The filters and the first draw

The filter bar has one listener too. It reads the data-filter value of the clicked button, saves it in filter, and redraws. The last line, render(), draws the list for the first time.

The complete app

Here is everything together. Add a task, tick one off, delete one, and try the filters. Press Reset to start again:

Live result: try it here

Your turn: challenges

  1. Clear completed. Add a button that removes all the done tasks in one click. (Hint: tasks = tasks.filter(t => !t.done).)
  2. Edit a task. Double-click a task's text to change it. (Hint: dblclick, and prompt or a small input.)
  3. Save your tasks. Make the tasks survive a page reload with localStorage (see the note below).
  4. Task count per filter. Show the number of tasks on each filter button, such as Active (2).
  5. Priority. Add a high property to tasks, and show high-priority tasks with a coloured border.
About saving with localStorage

Browsers have a small storage called localStorage that keeps text even after the page is closed. It works in your own .html files, but it does not work inside the live boxes of this book, so try it in your own file. Objects must be turned into text first with JSON.stringify, and back again with JSON.parse:

What you practised
  • Keeping the data in one place and redrawing the screen from it.
  • Building elements with createElement, append, and textContent.
  • classList.toggle(name, condition) and data- attributes.
  • A form with submit and preventDefault.
  • Event delegation with closest and matches.
  • Filtering arrays of objects with filter, and finding with find.
